Washing your Thanksgiving turkey spreads germs around the kitchen, but a USDA study shows skipping it is also a bad idea

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that washing a Thanksgiving turkey spreads germs, the USDA indicates.
  • Many families rinse the Thanksgiving turkey in the kitchen sink before it goes in the oven, because that is how a parent or grandparent always did it.
  • According to recent reports, “USDA research has found that washing or rinsing meat or poultry increases the risk for cross-contamination in the kitchen,” the agency’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that washing a Thanksgiving turkey spreads germs, the USDA indicates. But its 2019 test-kitchen study found the sink and poorly washed hands mattered more than splashes.

Many families rinse the Thanksgiving turkey in the kitchen sink before it goes in the oven, because that is how a parent or grandparent always did it. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) has been telling people for years to stop.

According to recent reports, “USDA research has found that washing or rinsing meat or poultry increases the risk for cross-contamination in the kitchen,” the agency’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) notes. Cooking the bird to the right temperature kills the germs, so washing it is “risky and not necessary for safety.”.

The research behind that advice holds a twist, though. The agency’s key experiment did not use turkeys.

When USDA-funded scientists filmed 300 home cooks preparing chicken thighs in test kitchens, many of the people who skipped washing their chicken still ended up with its bacteria in their salads. Their sinks and their hands spread it anyway.

Recent findings suggest that the study was carried out for FSIS by RTI International and North Carolina State University (NCSU), and its final report was dated August 20, 2019. It was the second round of a five-year FSIS consumer food safety research project.

The team set up eight test kitchens in the Raleigh-Durham area and in Lillington, a rural town in North Carolina. Every participant had said they wash or rinse raw poultry when cooking at home.

Recent findings suggest that before their appointments, 142 of them received three emails with USDA food safety messages. One said not to wash poultry and linked to a USDA video; one recommended separate cutting boards for raw meat and ready-to-eat food; and one was a USDA “Clean” infographic about not washing poultry and about washing hands and kitchen surfaces.

The other 158 participants received nothing.

It has been revealed that in the kitchen, six cameras recorded every move. Each person cooked chicken thighs and made a mixed green salad.

It has been revealed that what they did not know was that the chicken had been spiked with a harmless, traceable strain of E. coli called DH-5 alpha.

After the meal and the cleanup, the researchers swabbed the kitchen surfaces, tested the lettuce and counted where the marker bacteria had ended up.

It has been revealed that the messages changed what people did with the chicken. In the group that got the emails, 93% did not wash the chicken, compared with 39% in the group that did not.

It has been revealed that those who did wash it mostly rinsed it in the sink rather than submerging it. Asked why they wash chicken at home, 30% said they wanted to remove blood or slime, and 19% said it was how a family member did it.

Two-thirds of the participants who got the emails, 66%, noted the messages had changed how they cooked that day.

Then came the lab results. Lettuce from the salads carried the marker bacteria in 26% of the cooks who had washed their chicken and in 20% of those who had not. Washing made things somewhat worse, but skipping it was far from a fix.

Industry observers note that the researchers suspect hands were an notable factor. Handwashing was covered in one of the emails, but it did not change how participants washed their hands.

It has been revealed that of all the handwashing that should have happened before or during the meal, only 2% included every step the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends. The most common mistake was not rubbing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds.

Sources indicate that the report also found high levels of the marker in the sink. Microbes that reach the sink from the chicken, its packaging or contaminated hands “are a larger cause for concern than splashing contaminated chicken fluids onto the counter,” the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that A sink that is not cleaned properly can pass germs to whatever is rinsed in it next, such as lettuce or vegetables. Researchers have warned before that the sink deserves as much attention as your hands.

When the study was published in the Journal of Food Protection in 2022, Ellen Shumaker, its corresponding author at NC State, summed it up.

“Washing the chicken is still not a good idea, but this study demonstrates the need to focus on preventing contamination of sinks and emphasizing the importance of hand-washing and cleaning and sanitizing surfaces,” she noted.

Another finding: only 47% of all participants used a food thermometer on at least one chicken thigh.

In a release on November 13, the USDA reminded families that a food thermometer is the only way to know a turkey is done.

Recent findings suggest that the bird is safe at 165°F, checked in three places: the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the wing and the innermost part of the thigh. Stuffing is best cooked separately, and if it goes inside the turkey, its center must also reach 165°F.

Recent findings suggest that for a frozen turkey, the agency indicates never to thaw it on the counter. In the refrigerator, allow about 24 hours for every 4 to 5 pounds.

According to recent reports, in cold water, allow about 30 minutes per pound and change the water every 30 minutes. A fresh turkey should be bought one to two days before cooking.

Washing raw meat or poultry is not recommended, according to FSIS, and soap or detergent should never be used on it. Rinsing in salt water, vinegar or lemon juice does not make it safer either.

Kitchen surfaces should be cleaned first with hot, soapy water and then sanitized. Germs can linger: Campylobacter can survive in a kitchen for up to 4 hours and Salmonella for up to 32 hours, the agency states.

In a recent development, leftovers should go in the refrigerator within two hours. They keep for up to four days and should be reheated to 165°F.

Sources indicate that every year, USDA food safety specialists answer thousands of Thanksgiving questions through the agency’s Meat and Poultry Hotline. It is normally open Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern Time.

Sources indicate that on Thanksgiving Day, November 26, 2026, it will be open from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Eastern Time at 1-888-MPHotline (1-888-674-6854). Questions can also be sent by email to MPHotline@usda.gov.

Food is not the only holiday hazard in the house: earth.com has also looked at which Thanksgiving leftovers are safe to give your dog.

The information was obtained from the USDA’s November 13, 2026, Thanksgiving food safety release, the FSIS post From Freezer to Feast, the FSIS page Washing Food: Does it Promote Food Safety?, the 2019 final report of the poultry washing experiment and NC State’s 2022 release on the published study.

Tech Report: A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations.
  • Recent findings suggest that “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” indicates the narrator of the 1966 movie version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

Recent findings suggest that “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” indicates the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really major in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, claims Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”.

Recent findings suggest that in one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Recent findings suggest that smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson states. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”.

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, indicates Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

It has been revealed that “Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson states. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Industry observers note that some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand states, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”.

In a recent development, stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson states.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

In a recent development, A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson indicates. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.).

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

It has been revealed that pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as substantial as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

It has been revealed that once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Short-tailed albatrosses George and Geraldine returned to Midway Atoll for their 10th year together, offering hope for this endangered species.
  • Two short-tailed albatrosses known as George and Geraldine are back on Sand Island at Midway Atoll, which lies in the North Pacific.
  • Their arrival was confirmed in late October 2026, marking the 10th straight year the two have returned as a pair, according to the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Short-tailed albatrosses George and Geraldine returned to Midway Atoll for their 10th year together, offering hope for this endangered species.

Two short-tailed albatrosses known as George and Geraldine are back on Sand Island at Midway Atoll, which lies in the North Pacific.

Their arrival was confirmed in late October 2026, marking the 10th straight year the two have returned as a pair, according to the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP).

In a recent development, ACAP describes them as the only short-tailed albatrosses breeding in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Together they have raised and fledged at least five chicks.

Industry observers note that both birds were banded as chicks on Japan’s Torishima island. George hatched there in 2003 and has visited Midway since November 2006, when he was known as “Lonesome George.”.

According to recent reports, geraldine is thought to be a bird banded on Torishima in April 2008. She was first seen on Midway in early 2012, ACAP reported in 2024.

The two were first seen together in late 2016 and first shared a nest the following season.

That 2017/18 season, they incubated an egg laid by a black-footed albatross, and the chick fledged. Black-footed and Laysan albatrosses also nest on Sand Island.

In a recent development, geraldine’s sex was still listed as unconfirmed in 2018. She settled the question by laying the egg the two incubated in October 2023.

Recent findings suggest that before them, another short-tailed pair raised chicks on Midway’s Eastern Island, most recently in 2013/14. Its male was found dead there in November 2014.

George and Geraldine’s own first chick hatched on Jan. 3, 2019, and biologists banded it that May. It left its nest site earlier than expected, in late May, and became the first chick known to fledge from Sand Island.

Short-tailed albatross chicks hatch from late December through January, and each breeding cycle lasts about eight months.

Recent findings suggest that their next chick left in 2020. It walked across Sand Island before taking off over the water, likely to spend five or more years at sea.

“Nature has a way of reminding us that species and populations often have a remarkable capacity for resilience and fuel our hopes for recovering natural systems,” said Jonathan Plissner, then an island restoration specialist at Island Conservation, in 2020.

Not every season has worked. The 2021/22 egg did not hatch.

A chick that fledged in 2022/23 returned in April 2024 and displayed with one hatched in 2019/20. That November, two of their earlier chicks were photographed within a few feet of Geraldine as she incubated.

In late 2024, a fifth short-tailed albatross was also on Sand Island. The sub-adult, nicknamed Forest Bird, came from the same Torishima cohort as Geraldine and lived alone about a mile (1.6 kilometers) from the others.

George and Geraldine had no success in 2024/25. They bred again in 2025/26, when eight different short-tailed albatrosses were recorded on the atoll, three of them their offspring.

Those returning young birds may eventually start breeding on Midway themselves.

In Hawaiian, the short-tailed albatross is called makalena. Around the turn of the 20th century, feather hunters killed millions of them, nearly wiping out the species, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS).

It has been revealed that the agency listed the species as endangered throughout its range in 2000. A 2020 review estimated the population at 7,365 birds, growing about 8.9 percent a year.

It is the largest albatross in the North Pacific, with wings spanning about 7 to 7.5 feet (213 to 229 centimeters).

Sources indicate that short-tailed albatrosses begin breeding at five or six years old. Parents take turns on the egg and alternate foraging trips that can last two to three weeks.

Torishima, the main colony, is an active volcano. In 2010, a landslide there buried up to ten chicks.

Between 2008 and 2012, chicks moved from Torishima to Mukojima started a third colony.

It has been revealed that these albatrosses spend most of their lives at sea, ranging from China and Japan to Russia, Alaska and Canada. The highest concentrations occur around the Aleutian Islands and in the Bering Sea.

Birds that follow fishing boats can be hooked or tangled in longline gear and drown. Albatross chicks can also choke and die after eating plastic.

It has been revealed that on land, Midway brings its own threat. Mice were first seen attacking albatrosses on the atoll in December 2015.

The Midway Seabird Protection Project spread bait across Sand Island by helicopter on July 20 and 21, 2023. Crews also scattered bait by hand in sensitive areas and used bait boxes around buildings.

Sources indicate that by Aug. 15, mice were still being found, and eradication efforts were stopped.

The project then moved into what the USFWS calls a “Mitigation and Learning Phase.” A similar attempt on Gough Island also failed to remove mice that attack albatrosses and other seabirds.

The information was obtained from the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1120 w)

Industry News: How cranberries went from a Thanksgiving favorite to a symbol of stronger farming for the future

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Breeding cultivated cranberries with wild relatives may help protect future crops from extreme heat, frost and climate change.
  • Cranberries grow in some of the coldest parts of North America, but frost can still damage them.
  • In a recent development, in spring, frost can damage newly growing buds before they produce berries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Breeding cultivated cranberries with wild relatives may help protect future crops from extreme heat, frost and climate change.

Cranberries grow in some of the coldest parts of North America, but frost can still damage them.

In a recent development, in spring, frost can damage newly growing buds before they produce berries. In early fall, it can harm fruit that is still ripening.

Scientists crossed cultivated cranberries with a small wild relative from the far north called Vaccinium oxycoccos.

When exposed to cold, these new plants kept more genes involved in growth active than cultivated cranberries did.

The wild plant’s DNA could therefore be of use in breeding cranberries that handle cold weather better.

Audrey Dickinson, a researcher in agricultural genomics at the San Diego Botanic Garden and the Salk Institute, led the study.

Scientists from the USDA’s Agricultural Research Service in Chatsworth, Fresh Jersey, also took part.

It has been revealed that only leaves were sampled, over a span of minutes. Berries and harvests were not included.

The United States is the world’s largest cranberry producer. Strawberries are the only berry Americans eat more of. Most cranberries reach shoppers as juice or as sweetened dried fruit.

Berries can scald once the air passes about 90°F (32°C), and scalded fruit rots more easily. Frost, on the other hand, can leave the fruit soft.

Sources indicate that when growers were surveyed, New Jersey producers named heat tolerance first. Wisconsin and British Columbia growers named frost tolerance.

One round of cranberry breeding takes seven to eight years. Most varieties are only a few generations away from wild vines. Wheat breeders, for one, have borrowed heat tolerance from wild relatives.

Sources indicate that the small cranberry grows across the cold far north. As its name suggests, its berries are smaller than those of the farmed species.

The two plants look different, but they cross easily. Gene by gene, their published genomes line up closely.

Wild plants for this work were collected in southeastern Alaska in 1996. In 1998, four of them were crossed with the farmed varieties Stevens, Ben Lear and Pilgrim.

According to recent reports, for three days, the team kept Stevens and the four hybrid lines at 70°F (21°C). Then the plants went into incubators.

The heated plants reached 117°F (47°C) in 30 minutes, while the chilled plants cooled to 37°F (3°C) over 95 minutes.

The team clipped leaves three times and froze them in liquid nitrogen. Their RNA was read with Oxford Nanopore sequencing, which kept the wild and farmed gene copies apart.

It has been revealed that plants need proteins to grow. Ribosomes assemble those proteins, and the genes that build ribosomes are tied to growth.

Photosynthesis genes, used by leaves to turn sunlight into energy-rich sugars, are tied to growth as well.

Ribosome gene activity declined during the cold test in both Stevens and the hybrids, but the decline was greater in Stevens.

Photosynthesis gene activity increased in the hybrids but decreased in Stevens.

Sources indicate that basic cell work, the researchers suggested, kept going in the hybrids under stress. In Stevens, that work was reduced. Total photosynthesis gene activity, however, stayed higher in Stevens under every condition.

The two groups differed much more in cold than in heat. In the cold test, 18 broad sets of related genes behaved differently between hybrids and Stevens. In the heat test, only one set did.

The team linked this to where the parents come from. The farmed cranberry is native farther south. It may photosynthesize best at warmer temperatures.

A chill that stresses Stevens may be closer to normal growing weather for its wild Alaskan cousin.

The four hybrid lines did not respond in the same way. Gene activity differed more among the lines than between the hybrids as a group and Stevens.

It has been revealed that two lines with the same Stevens parent also differed from each other. The wild parents were therefore likely a major source of this variation.

In the cold test, two lines demonstrated an unusual pattern. At 60 minutes their gene activity shot up. By 95 minutes it had fallen, although the air was still getting colder. In Stevens, large changes continued to the end.

The team sees that rise and fall as a possible sign of efficient adjustment to cold. Results in the heat test were different.

After 30 minutes of heat, Stevens showed the smallest overall change of all the plants.

Some hybrids may cope with cold better than Stevens, then, yet cope with heat worse.

In a recent development, heat and cold tolerance may need separate tests in breeding programs. Coping with one is no guarantee for the other.

Sources indicate that at room temperature, the hybrids mostly took after Stevens. Some 57% of compared genes tracked the farmed parent, against 14% for the Alaskan one.

Recent findings suggest that about 22% of genes were less active in the hybrids than in either parent, many of them tied to photosynthesis. A cold acclimation gene called WCOR413 was among them.

That could hint at hybrid weakness, a known risk when two separately evolved genomes are merged.

In a recent development, chloroplasts may be part of the explanation. These green structures are where photosynthesis takes place. Many photosynthesis proteins are coded in the cell’s main DNA but work inside chloroplasts.

It has been revealed that chloroplasts also carry a small amount of their own DNA. The two sets of DNA must work together. A mismatch between them could disrupt photosynthesis genes.

To keep the two in step, the authors suggested crossing hybrids back to a farmed cranberry mother several times.

The experiments were short. Only the first 30 minutes of heat and the first 95 minutes of cold were studied. Longer or repeated stress may produce different results.

Gene activity is also only a partial guide to which proteins a plant makes.

In a recent development, the two temperature experiments were also quite different. The heat was intense enough to potentially kill the plants, while the cold temperature was still within the range that cranberries normally experience outdoors.

Industry observers note that the researchers also did not measure plant survival, growth or berry production. It is still unclear whether a calmer gene response means a hardier plant.

For Dickinson, the study also highlights why protecting wild plants matters.

“These results highlight the importance of conserving crop wild relatives in their natural habitats and in collections,” she wrote.

Future research could test whether these gene patterns match real frost and heat tolerance in the field.

The study is published in the journal Plants, People, Planet.

The Adventurer is currently repositioning to South America ahead of the debut of Terra Nova Expeditions in Antarctica.

In a recent development, replacing the RMS St. Helena, the 127-passenger ship is scheduled to offer a series of expedition cruises from Argentina for the startup brand.

After a technical call in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, the 1972-built vessel started a trans-Atlantic crossing on November 13, 2026.

The Adventurer is now scheduled to arrive in Montevideo later this month before heading to Ushuaia to kick off its maiden season for Terra Nova.

For its inaugural voyage, the ship will offer a ten-night expedition as part of Terra Nova’s “Classic Antarctica” itinerary.

The tech giant said the cruise highlights exploration of the Antarctic Peninsula’s icebergs and glaciers, as well as abundant wildlife encounters.

As previously reported by Cruise Industry News, Terra Nova had to change its launch aims due to conflicts in the Middle East.

The firm stated that the St. Helena could not reposition from the Persian Gulf safely or on schedule because of the ongoing situation in the region.

As a result, it finalized a new charter contract after several months of work, securing the Adventurer as an alternative vessel for three Antarctica seasons.

Before embarking on its repositioning voyage to South America, the ship underwent a series of upgrades in Europe.

In addition to new soft furnishings, the work included remodeling the bar and lounge areas and adding a jacuzzi and a new sauna.

Originally built as a Danish ferry, the Adventurer was converted into an expedition vessel in 2008 and last sailed for G Adventures. The company withdrew the ship from its fleet in 2025, later selling it to Vestland Classic Cruises.

Renamed Vestland Adventurer, the vessel remained out of service in Northern Europe for the past year.

Digital twins of cancer patients could help doctors find better treatments

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Digital twins of breast tumors could help doctors predict treatment responses and identify potentially effective alternative drugs.
  • Sources indicate that ask a chatbot-style AI which drug to give a cancer patient, and it may offer an answer without providing a transparent, scientifically grounded explanation.
  • In London, a team took the opposite route: a program built from logic rather than statistics, which a doctor can open up and read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Digital twins of breast tumors could help doctors predict treatment responses and identify potentially effective alternative drugs.

Sources indicate that ask a chatbot-style AI which drug to give a cancer patient, and it may offer an answer without providing a transparent, scientifically grounded explanation. That, the researchers said, has left many doctors skeptical of such tools.

In London, a team took the opposite route: a program built from logic rather than statistics, which a doctor can open up and read.

Run on virtual copies of 31 real tumors, the program predicted whether a patient’s treatment would work 74% of the time.

For 12 of the 13 patients whose incomplete response the model correctly predicted, it identified at least one additional drug that might have helped.

Jasmin Fisher of the UCL Cancer Institute led the work, with Pedro Victori as first author and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute.

Every result is a simulation checked against records from a trial that has already ended, and the drugs it suggested were not tested in the patients it picked them for.

“We see our computer model as an aid for existing cancer clinical practice, not an alternative to it,” Fisher stated.

The cancer in question is triple-negative breast cancer, about 15% of breast cancers.

Sources indicate that its cells lack the three receptors that most breast cancer drugs aim at, so hormone therapies don’t work. About 40% of patients die within five years of diagnosis.

Instead of training on patient data, the team hand-built a map of how the disease works. They read 191 research papers and drew 142 genes, proteins and cell processes as nodes.

Then they linked the nodes with 379 arrows that say which one switches which on or off, and let each node be off, low or fully on.

The map includes the machinery that repairs broken DNA, which chemotherapy and the drug olaparib attack. It also includes the machinery of cell division, which the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel jams.

Two output nodes sum it up: whether the cancer cells die, and whether they keep multiplying.

Before applying the model to individual tumors, the team checked it against 160 laboratory results from 33 other papers and adjusted it until it reproduced all of them.

In a recent development, the patients came from PARTNER, a trial run by Jean Abraham’s team in Cambridge. Its patients, all with triple-negative breast cancer, received four chemotherapy drugs before surgery, with or without olaparib.

For 31 of them, the team had full genome sequences of the tumor.

Each patient’s mutations and missing or duplicated genes were loaded into the map to make a digital twin of the tumor.

According to recent reports, A patient with a disabled BRCA1 gene, for instance, had that node fixed at zero. Then the twin was given the same treatment the patient had received, and the program reported whether the cells died.

Recent findings suggest that the predictions matched the real outcomes in 23 of 31 cases. The program was right for 10 of the 14 patients whose cancer disappeared completely, and for 13 of the 17 whose cancer did not.

Only those 23 accurate twins were used for what came next.

The team then took the 13 twins that resisted treatment and switched off every gene in the map, one at a time. They watched for the switch that tipped the simulated cells into dying.

According to recent reports, twelve of the 13 had one. For 10, the program predicted a complete response, eight with a single added drug and two with a pair.

The most broadly useful target was a protein called ATM, which helps cells repair DNA damage; blocking it was predicted to produce a complete response in seven patients.

The other twins pointed to drugs that have passed phase 2 trials, including inhibitors of Chk1, ATR, MEK, mTOR and Wee1.

Fisher mentioned the point is to give a doctor a lead, not an order.

“In practice, the treatment option recommended by our model may, under closer scrutiny, be discounted by the clinician – for example, if they view the drug as too toxic,” she mentioned.

“But it may also lead them to explore, and eventually settle on, a third option which they might otherwise not have arrived at.”.

The one tumor for which the program could not identify an effective additional treatment contained three distinct populations of cancer cells.

Spatial RNA data demonstrated three groups of cells with different gene activity sitting in different parts of the tumor.

Sources indicate that simulated separately, each of the three had targets the whole-tumor model had missed. One of them, a lower-grade carcinoma, was predicted to respond completely to an added drug.

A sample taken after treatment held a fourth group unlike any of the first three, carrying two changes the model flags as resistance.

The team also pulled the 29 genes the program had flagged as targets and tested them as a signature in a public database of breast cancer patients.

Among patients with the basal subtype treated with chemotherapy alone, those carrying mutations in the signature genes lived longer.

Thirty-one patients is a small group, and the authors wrote that it limits how finely they can slice the results.

The model is right about three times in four, which also means it is wrong once in four. The twins that failed were set aside before the drug search began.

The map knows only what 191 papers told it, so it can’t propose a mechanism nobody has published.

It also ignores the immune cells and other tissue around a tumor, which matter most for immunotherapy. And it models the drugs used in PARTNER rather than the newer antibody-drug conjugates now in use.

Recent findings suggest that each twin was built from DNA alone. The authors wrote that adding gene activity and protein data would likely sharpen the predictions.

The framework is designed to be updated as a patient’s tumor changes under treatment.

Determining whether the suggested drugs actually benefit patients will require a clinical trial in which the model’s predictions inform treatment decisions.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Reports Medicine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Maya people had a toxic relationship with the color red—quite literally, according to fresh research. The fresh analysis of the Yucatán Peninsula during the Maya era identified astronomically spiked levels of mercury, which might have contributed to the collapse of Maya culture.

“The mercury data was crazy,” Matt Waters, an environmental sciences professor and paleolimnologist at Auburn University, said in a university statement about the unexpected discovery on the peninsula. “Off the charts. These mercury levels aren’t normal.”.

Matt Waters led a study published in Science Advances that explored sediment samples collected at two lakes—Lago Coba and Cenote Xcach—showing the intense spike in mercury (Hg) levels ranging from around 40 C.E. to 800 C.E.

“We show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation,” the authors wrote, adding that the heightened pollution coincides with aquatic food collapse, “confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.”.

While Waters isn’t saying mercury caused the collapse of the Maya civilization, he also doesn’t want to ignore its impact. “It’s been confirmed that drought was an issue, deforestation was an issue, erosion was an issue, overpopulation was an issue, and feeding the population was probably an issue,” he said. “This study adds the impact of water quality. Let’s put that in the list. That’s what our study does. It establishes that list and moves it forward.”.

The study actually began as part of a National Science Foundation project focused on harmful algal blooms, but a then-graduate student and study co-author, Savanna Wooten, suggested also testing for heavy metals. Sediment coring from the lake bottoms pulled up mud from thousands of years ago that contained the intense mercury spikes during the Classic Maya Period, which were then followed by an abrupt decline.

The powerfully high mercury concentration lasted for hundreds of years, and Waters believes the sudden change at the base level likely moved up the food web, impacting fish and other larger creatures. Not only would eating fish or drinking water have exposed humans to the toxic levels, but there may have even been fewer fish to catch. “They would have seen a strange color change in the water,” Waters told Live Science, “and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein.”.

According to recent reports, waters linked to a study he’d worked on with a team from the University of Florida in the late 1990s that found a gap in ostracod shells during a specific period from Coba, correlating the missing shell timing to the rise in mercury. Further investigation into the cores found that declines in biological markers occurred throughout. “The algae was killed,” he noted. “The cyanobacteria, they tanked. Purple sulfur bacteria, vanished. The biological community completely changed.”.

The people “experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries.”.

Recent findings suggest that the source of that mercury was cinnabar, they believe, a vibrant red mineral made up of 86 percent mercury that Maya culture viewed as a sacred pigment. “This was not like mercury raining down from the sky,” Waters mentioned. “This was not a regional thing. It was concentrated.”.

Sources indicate that maya loved cinnabar, using the bright red in pottery, murals, temple walls, and burials. To keep up with demand, they heavily imported it, especially around Coba and Xcach. “It’s common knowledge that there was trade in obsidian, in jade, and beautiful stones, and weaponry,” Waters stated. “I think this could start a conversation that cinnabar could have been a major trade commodity.”.

It may also show a highly toxic love affair that contributed to Maya struggles.

Breaking: Putting down your phone may have less to do with willpower than you think

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Problematic internet use may affect over 10% of people worldwide, prompting experts to call for safer digital platforms.
  • Recent findings suggest that you pick up your phone to answer one message.
  • That lost hour is usually put down to poor willpower.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Problematic internet use may affect over 10% of people worldwide, prompting experts to call for safer digital platforms.

Recent findings suggest that you pick up your phone to answer one message. An hour later, you’re still scrolling through videos you never meant to watch.

That lost hour is usually put down to poor willpower. A report from an international panel of experts treats it instead as a global public health concern.

According to their estimate, problematic internet use may affect more than 10% of people worldwide.

Part of the blame, the authors argue, lies with the way apps and websites are designed by technology companies.

The report comes from the Lancet Psychiatry Commission on global action on problematic usage of the internet.

Psychiatrists, psychologists and public health researchers from several countries began the work in February 2023.

In a recent development, people who had struggled with their own internet use were involved from the start. They served as advisers throughout the project.

No latest experiment was run. Instead, the commission reviewed existing studies and turned the findings into recommendations for governments.

Recent findings suggest that some online habits are already recognized as medical conditions. Gaming disorder and gambling disorder both appear in the World Health Organization’s ICD-11 classification.

Compulsive social media use and problem online shopping haven’t received that status yet.

Industry observers note that then there’s cyberchondria. That’s when someone keeps searching their symptoms online and grows more anxious with every search.

Industry observers note that not everyone who spends hours online has a disorder. The researchers describe a spectrum, running from useful, productive time online to habits that seriously disrupt daily life.

Zsolt Demetrovics is a professor of psychology at ELTE Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest and at Flinders University in Australia.

He sat on the commission’s four-member steering group, which was chaired by Naomi Fineberg of the University of Hertfordshire.

“Digital technologies are now woven into almost every aspect of modern life and bring enormous benefits,” Demetrovics stated.

Recent findings suggest that the commission isn’t trying to get people offline. Its focus is on stopping everyday use from turning harmful.

Internet use is now reported by an estimated 6 billion people, or roughly three-quarters of the world’s total population.

Social media platforms are used for an average of 3.5 hours per day by people aged 16 to 24.

Rates of problematic use above 10% have often been reported in meta-analyses that included pandemic-era studies.

A prevalence of around 7% had been estimated for the period before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Estimates vary depending on how researchers define and measure problematic internet use. One pandemic-era study put the figure at 25%, but stricter criteria brought it down to 7.9%.

Researchers still cannot say whether the problem is growing worldwide. Even the lowest estimates, however, represent millions of people.

Studies suggest that gaming disorder affects 2% to 12% of people. Around 5% struggle with social media use, while 16% struggle with compulsive online shopping.

Problems with gambling, gaming and pornography are more common among males.

Females more often struggle with social media, online shopping and cyberchondria.

Higher rates have also been reported in low-income and middle-income countries than in wealthier ones.

Industry observers note that young people seem especially vulnerable. Brain changes during the teenage years can make it harder to control impulses, which may be part of the reason.

Sources indicate that think about what happens when a video ends. Another one starts on its own, and there’s always something else waiting.

Features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and personalized recommendations can make it hard to stop.

The commission also flagged unpredictable rewards, gambling-like features, pop-ups and tools that invite people to compare themselves with others.

Andrea Czakó, a senior research fellow in psychology at Flinders University, was one of the report’s authors.

“Many digital products are intentionally designed to capture and hold our attention,” Czakó mentioned.

The ever-increasing power of artificial intelligence to strengthen such designs and algorithms was flagged as a further concern.

The effects of AI chatbots on young people were described by the authors as barely investigated.

Most gambling and gaming and social media platforms are owned by a relatively small number of transnational corporations.

Ownership by a handful of gatekeeper firms was seen by the commission as both a challenge and an opportunity.

Powerful technology companies have tended to resist regulation. Natural checkpoints in the market could nonetheless be required to help enforce international standards.

A similar argument about design and young people was made in a recent Lancet series on digital media.

Problematic internet use frequently co-occurs with ADHD, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbances and eating disorders.

But which problem comes first? Most studies examined people at a single point in time, making it difficult to determine which problem came first.

In gambling disorder, however, other mental disorders were found to precede the gambling problem in about 75% of instances.

Less evidence exists for the direction of such relationships in other forms of problematic internet use.

Some longitudinal studies have linked online social activity in young people to subsequent ADHD symptoms, but not the reverse.

Poor sleep may help explain why problem social media use is linked to depression and anxiety.

Separate research has tied screen use in bed to a higher risk of insomnia among young adults.

Recent findings suggest that in the commission’s view, these problems can feed each other. Low mood may push someone online, and heavy use may then make things worse.

How much does problematic internet use cost society? Few estimates of the economic costs or societal burdens were found to exist.

A worked example for the UK was therefore produced by the commission using a prevalence-based cost-of-illness approach.

A base case of about 5% prevalence and around 3.3 million affected individuals was assumed for this example.

The total annual economic cost of problematic use in the UK was conservatively put at approximately £10 to £12 billion.

That amount corresponds to about 0.4% of UK gross domestic product.

About half of the total was found to come from hard-to-see losses such as foregone productivity and quality-of-life decrements.

Most of the burden of problematic internet use was therefore judged to fall outside traditional health-care spending.

The precise figures were acknowledged to be open to debate by the authors of the model.

Gaming disorder had been estimated in one earlier study to cost South Korea approximately $3.5 billion per year.

The commission surveyed addiction societies in 38 countries across Europe, Asia, Oceania, the Americas and Africa.

According to recent reports, in 31 of them, treatments such as cognitive behavioral therapy were available. This therapy helps people notice and change unhelpful patterns of thinking and behavior.

Yet 30 of the 38 societies said a lack of professional certification was a major gap.

Cognitive behavioral therapy has the strongest evidence so far, especially when it’s delivered in groups.

Still, few clinical trials have tested treatments for problematic internet use, and their quality is often low.

Regulatory frameworks have been used with success within similar areas of public health and safety such as alcohol and gambling.

A wide range of measures with potential for the regulation of problematic internet use was suggested on that basis.

Safety by design was described in the report as a key principle for regulating digital products and platforms.

Age restrictions and product disclosure of risks and harms and the enforcement of safety and quality standards were also recommended.

Australia was the first country to pass a law restricting social media access for children under 16. Platforms there must take reasonable steps to keep under-16s from holding accounts.

In the UK, the Age-Appropriate Design Code recommends limiting features such as autoplay and infinite scroll for children.

In the US, the Surgeon General has called for warning labels on social media platforms. A separate trial has tested how teenagers respond to such warnings.

Countries including Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea and China have introduced restrictions on online gaming time.

The outcomes of these policies have been controversial and their effectiveness has been questioned in recent research.

Industry observers note that loot boxes, which hand out random rewards in video games, have been classified as gambling in Belgium. Enforcement of the resulting ban has been difficult.

Restrictive school smartphone policies might reduce smartphone usage during the school day according to recent UK data.

No significant difference in overall phone usage or mental wellbeing among young people was made by such policies.

Some projects are trying prevention instead of restriction.

A European project called BootStRaP recruits young people through schools and offers them flexible support through an app.

“The challenge is finding ways to reduce harms while preserving the many benefits of being connected,” Demetrovics mentioned.

Estimates of prevalence were acknowledged to vary substantially according to the definitions and assessment instruments and thresholds and regions used.

According to recent reports, proxy variables such as screen time have been used even in high-quality studies. Screen time is not equivalent to problematic use.

The effectiveness of many of the regulatory policies described in the report is yet to be fully evaluated.

The existing evidence base was nonetheless considered sufficient by the commission to justify immediate national and internationally coordinated action.

Large-scale longitudinal studies with standardised assessment were called for to clarify the course and outcomes of problematic use.

Future research could test whether restricting engagement features such as autoplay and infinite scroll reduces problematic internet use.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet Psychiatry.

#134609. Donkeys help families survive droughts, but governments often overlook them

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1483 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Donkeys help families survive droughts, but governments often overlook them

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Donkeys help East African families survive severe droughts, yet governments and aid organizations often overlook their essential needs.
  • Recent findings suggest that families in East Africa depend on donkeys for many everyday tasks.
  • In a drought their job gets even more crucial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Donkeys help East African families survive severe droughts, yet governments and aid organizations often overlook their essential needs.

Recent findings suggest that families in East Africa depend on donkeys for many everyday tasks. The animals carry water, feed for livestock, and household belongings. They have also been part of local culture for generations.

In a drought their job gets even more crucial. Once the water close to home has dried up, donkeys trek long distances to bring it back.

Yet when drought relief arrives, donkeys are rarely part of it. Aid has tended to go to the food-producing animals, and donkey-owning households end up worse off for it.

A team from the University of Portsmouth, Maasai Mara University and Haramaya University looked at how far that neglect goes.

In a recent development, they went through 77 documents and talked with 41 people on the ground. Donkeys, it turned out, are mostly missing, from the policies right down to the vet schools.

From 2020 to 2023 East Africa was hit by drought. Crops failed widely and some places lost up to 70% of livestock.

Around 26 million people were threatened with food shortages, and conflict over the dwindling resources went up.

Many of the worst affected families are pastoralists, meaning their living depends on herds that often move with them.

Donkeys have been part of that life since they were domesticated in Africa thousands of years ago.

Industry observers note that when nearby sources dry up, the water a donkey brings back keeps people, crops and herds going. Donkeys also get people to health facilities, aid distribution centers and markets.

Kenya and Ethiopia both rely heavily on them. Ethiopia has about 10.8 million donkeys, and Kenya around 1.2 million.

Professor Leanne Proops works on animal behavior and welfare at the University of Portsmouth and supervised the project.

“Working donkeys are a lifeline for many communities during drought, helping people access water, transport essential supplies and sustain their livelihoods,” said Proops.

“Yet their contribution is largely overlooked in the policies and support systems designed to help communities cope with these crises.”.

Of the 77 documents, 51 were Kenyan and 26 Ethiopian, issued anywhere from 1964 up to 2025.

According to recent reports, animal health, agriculture, climate change, disaster risk and water were the areas covered. Equids, that is donkeys, horses and mules, came up in just 17.

Quite often the donkey got one mention in a species list and was absent from the rest of the policy.

According to recent reports, “Livestock” was a word used a lot, but most documents never said what species it took in. In reality it meant cattle, sheep and goats.

Donkeys, on the occasions they did appear, sat outside conventional livestock under labels such as “working animals” or “emerging livestock.”.

Not one of the documents made a link between donkeys and drought, even though camels were mentioned in that role.

In a recent development, on welfare the picture is not much better. Kenya’s Animal Welfare and Protection Bill has been in deliberation since 2019 without being enacted.

Up until 2025, Ethiopia’s criminal code only made cruelty an offense when it happened where the public could see.

A 2025 proclamation now prohibits overloading or overworking any working animal, though no penalties are set out in that part.

References to animals in the policies were heavily based on use, with meat, milk, hides and exports driving them. Kenya’s 2024 Livestock Bill does define donkeys as draught animals but welfare hardly features.

The interviews pointed the same way. If a drought is forecast, preparedness looks kick in with worming and vaccination for the other livestock.

“The donkeys were generally left out. Nobody was thinking about them,” one participant in Kenya told the researchers.

Later on, supplementary feed rations get handed out in both countries and again the donkeys are not counted.

A participant in Ethiopia stated that when fodder runs short, “the priority is not for donkeys, not for mules, just for animals with salvage value.”.

It has been revealed that in the only program one Kenyan participant had worked on with donkeys included, they got rabies vaccination and no food. The rest of the animals were counted for supplementary feeding.

Participants also noted that droughts are far more frequent than before. Money often comes towards the end, when much has died.

Pastoralists summed this up in their own words: “money comes with the vultures.”.

It has been revealed that dr. Emily Haddy, lead author of the paper, did the work at Portsmouth and is now at the University of Nottingham.

“Recognising donkeys in livestock and disaster planning is not just an animal welfare problem,” mentioned Haddy.

“By including working donkeys in drought preparedness and emergency responses, governments and aid organisations can help protect animal welfare and strengthen community resilience.”.

Sources indicate that the veterinarians taking part spoke of getting little or no training on donkeys. One participant in Kenya said they try to extrapolate from horses, which does not always hold.

“We try to extrapolate what we know from the horse to the donkey, which is not always true,” the participant said.

Industry observers note that vets specializing in donkeys are few and tend to be in urban areas such as Nairobi. Pastoralist communities therefore often have no access, and lose animals that could have been treated.

Medications suitable for donkeys are also in short supply, particularly anesthesia and pain relief.

“I don’t even think there is any company in Kenya which makes feeds for donkeys,” another participant said.

Recent findings suggest that it should be noted the vets interviewed were older graduates. Donkey medicine in the Kenyan vet curriculum has recently improved, though its effect on the ground may take time.

According to participants, the priority for government is animals bringing in foreign currency directly, through sale of meat and hides.

Industry observers note that the services of a donkey are largely invisible. That makes them hard to quantify and keeps them out of national economic reports.

Recent findings suggest that one participant described a child-focused relief scheme for milk. Donkeys play a vital role in that milk chain, but they were not taken into account.

“They see the human being first, and they see the cattle, the producer of the milk, and the consumer of the milk, the in-between connection they don’t see,” the participant said.

Donkey deaths are also not systematically recorded, so they usually do not appear when authorities list the animals that died.

International guidelines do mention working equids. The Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards, aimed at livestock projects in humanitarian crises, include them as pack animals.

The World Organisation for Animal Health gives advice on managing equids during feed shortage too. These were poorly reflected in the national documents.

Professor Tesfaheywet Zeryehun of Haramaya University put the two kinds of welfare side by side.

“Our findings reinforce the fact that donkey welfare cannot be separated from human wellbeing,” mentioned Zeryehun.

“In drought-prone communities, protecting working donkeys is equally about protecting the livelihoods, resilience and dignity of the families who depend on them.”.

“Their contribution must therefore be recognized in policies and emergency preparedness programs.”.

Recent findings suggest that documents had to be online and in English to be included. That likely cut the Ethiopian count, as many are in Amharic.

Only one pastoralist representative from Ethiopia was interviewed, so those views are probably underrepresented. Fewer than 15% of participants were women.

People were found by snowballing through the authors’ own contacts, and that could bring some selection bias with it.

It has been revealed that what’s missing above all is hard evidence on how much donkeys are worth economically. Several interviewees felt numbers on that are what would capture the minds of policy makers.

In a recent development, the authors recommend that equids be explicitly included in livestock definitions. Doing that would make donkeys eligible for the feed and veterinary support that other livestock can get.

They also suggest fodder reserves kept for donkeys, donkey modules in vet training and welfare laws that are actually enforced.

The impact of severe drought on donkey health is named as a research priority.

According to recent reports, dr. David Obiero of Maasai Mara University noted the gaps reach beyond policy itself.

“The lack of recognition of working donkeys extends beyond policy into veterinary training, access to healthcare and vaccination programmes,” noted Obiero.

Recent findings suggest that “These animals are vital to community livelihoods, yet the systems designed to support livestock often overlook them. Addressing these gaps is essential to supporting pastoralist communities during time of drought and beyond.”.

With recurrent droughts expected to intensify, the animal fetching the water is still largely outside the plans to help.

The full study was published in the Journal of Rural Studies.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks.
  • Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs).
  • At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks. With the ability to sift through unfathomably large data sets, AI could help detect cancers in their infancy, unlock some of the most enduring mysteries of mathematics, and even help contain the beating nuclear heart of future fusion reactors.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs). Even the everyday LLMs that now litter our digital lives—Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok—can aid and abet some of the most dangerous actors on the planet.

At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S. government. Typically, GAO turns its investigative gaze on efforts to limit fraud and wasteful spending in the government itself, but in a upcoming tactic at the urging of U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the office instead performed real-world tests on the platform to see if these four popular AI models would aid in planning a terrorist attack.

Sources indicate that “A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan, incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, mentioned in a press statement. “Today’s fresh report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”.

GAO conducted this test in the spring this year, and earlier this week reported some disturbing results. Two of the platforms, according to an official GAO release, provided guidance on building and detonating an improvised explosion device, or IED, and two other AI models showing differing methods for targeting the electrical grid. Within 12 hours, all four models also gamed through potential locations and methods for carrying out such an attack.

According to recent reports, although these violent lines of questioning triggered each platform’s safeguards, GAO got around them using common safeguard-bypassing techniques. Additionally, they confirmed the validity of the information provided with experts. The results of this investigation were published in a 61-page report that will be central to future senate hearings on AI safety.

It has been revealed that “We set out to do two different types of evil,” GAO director Kevin Walsh remarked in an interview posted on YouTube. “The first type is we wanted to create a bomb. And we didn’t just want to know how to create a bomb, we wanted it to help pick out a target, a location, and a time, and to give us instructions all the way…Evil scenario two, we wanted to do a bunch of economic damage, and in both cases that ended up being targeting the electrical grid.”.

In one case, Walsh reports that one AI model would refuse to answer questions or divert the user to more safe behaviors but said that “it wasn’t always successful.” Walsh says that companies theoretically call law enforcement when suspicious activity is detected, but whether that occurs and at what frequency is uncertain.

“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the report concludes. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”.

It has been revealed that the GAO officially released these terrorist-abetting findings on November 18, 2026, the same day Anthropic, creators of Claude, went public on the stock exchange. Despite the company’s own admission of AI being an existential threat to humanity, its IPO at one point reached a meteoric a $2 trillion valuation before dipping back down to a (measly) $1.6 trillion.

An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Sources indicate that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sources indicate that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

It has been revealed that state officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, notes environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

In a recent development, in 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier claims. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

Recent findings suggest that that waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this upcoming climate normal.

According to recent reports, 1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

According to recent reports, but the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Recent findings suggest that not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” claims Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

In a recent development, but there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

It has been revealed that the El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

Industry observers note that on February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

In a recent development, “We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves states now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

Recent findings suggest that the neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves states. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

According to recent reports, he reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier notes. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk glitch,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

According to recent reports, california’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier claims. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

In a recent development, those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

According to recent reports, such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a massive boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Recent findings suggest that precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

Sources indicate that it’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, indicates Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

In a recent development, then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Industry observers note that those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

According to recent reports, segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

According to recent reports, “Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she notes. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

According to recent reports, but, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.
