💡 Key Takeaways
  • The letter, never mailed to his daughter, was not published in full in English until 1817.
  • A popular Thanksgiving story holds that Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey, not the bald eagle, to be the national bird of the United States.
  • In a recent development, the story traces back to a letter dated January 26, 1784, and addressed to his daughter, Sarah Bache.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The letter, never mailed to his daughter, was not published in full in English until 1817. The bald eagle became the national bird by law only in 2024.

A popular Thanksgiving story holds that Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey, not the bald eagle, to be the national bird of the United States. It is a good story, but it is not what Franklin actually wrote.

In a recent development, the story traces back to a letter dated January 26, 1784, and addressed to his daughter, Sarah Bache. In it, he poked fun at the eagle on the badge of the Society of the Cincinnati and said a few kind words about the turkey. In that letter, he never proposes the turkey as a national symbol.

According to the editors of his papers, Franklin never even sent the letter to his daughter. And the bald eagle itself was officially designated the national bird by law only in 2024, more than two centuries later.

Industry observers note that when Franklin wrote the letter, the bald eagle was already on the Great Seal of the United States. It had been adopted for the seal on June 20, 1782.

In the winter of 1783 to 1784, Franklin, the American minister, was too ill to travel and isolated at Passy, in France, according to the editors of his papers.

Recent findings suggest that on January 26, he saw the founding document of the Society of the Cincinnati, a hereditary order of American army officers. John Paul Jones had sent it to him along with a pamphlet attacking the society.

The letter that Franklin wrote that same day was, in the view of the editors of The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, a satire meant as a public essay.

Addressing it to his daughter, with whom, the editors note, he never corresponded about politics, made it look like a private note.

He took aim at the idea of passing honors down to children. He objected to “an order of hereditary Knights, in direct opposition to the solemnly declared sense of their country.”.

According to recent reports, he even did the math. In nine generations, he wrote, a member’s share in his descendant would be “but a 512th part.”.

In a recent development, the birds come up near the end, when Franklin turns to the society’s badges, which had been made in France. “To me they seem tolerably done; but all such things are criticised,” he wrote.

It has been revealed that some critics, he reported, disliked the Latin mottos. “Others object to the bald eagle, as looking too much like a Dindon or turkey,” he wrote, using the French word for turkey.

Sources indicate that then Franklin gave his own opinion. “For my own part I wish the bald eagle had not been chosen as the representative of our country,” he wrote. “He is a bird of bad moral character. He does not get his living honestly.”.

In a recent development, he described the eagle sitting on a dead tree, “too lazy to fish for himself,” while it watched another bird, which he called the fishing hawk. When that bird caught a fish and carried it toward its nest, he wrote, the eagle “pursues him, and takes it from him.”.

Sources indicate that he went further. “Besides he is a rank coward,” Franklin wrote. The “little king bird not bigger than a sparrow attacks him boldly and drives him out of the district.”.

Recent findings suggest that only then does Franklin praise the turkey. He wrote that he was “not displeased” that the figure on the badge was not recognizable as a bald eagle and looked more like a turkey.

“For in truth, the turkey is in comparison a much more respectable bird, and withal a true original native of America,” he wrote. Eagles, he noted, “have been found in all countries, but the turkey was peculiar to ours.”.

He did not spare the turkey entirely. He called it “a little vain and silly,” though “not the worse emblem for that,” and “a bird of courage” that would attack a grenadier of the British guards who dared to invade its farmyard “with a red coat on.”.

It has been revealed that nowhere in the letter does Franklin ask for the turkey to replace the eagle on the seal or anywhere else. The comparison is part of a joke about a badge.

Industry observers note that according to the editors of his papers, Franklin showed the letter only to his grandsons before sending it, around March 1784, to the abbé Morellet in France to translate it into French. Morellet advised against publishing it. Franklin agreed and promised it would not appear while he was alive.

A partial French translation came out in Paris in 1790, months after Franklin’s death. The full English text was not published until 1817, when William Temple Franklin included it in his edition of Franklin’s writings.

In other words, the letter that so many people now quote was almost unknown in Franklin’s lifetime.

The bald eagle’s official title came with a bill that Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota introduced on June 20, 2024, exactly 242 years after the eagle was adopted for the Great Seal.

In a recent development, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent in July 2024, and the House approved it by voice vote on December 16, 2024. It was signed into law on December 23, 2024, as Public Law 118-206.

Sources indicate that the law adds a new section to the U.S. Code. It reads: “The bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) is the national bird.”.

In its findings, Congress noted that the bald eagle is unique to North America and that federal, state and local governments, nonprofit groups and individuals had all contributed to its recovery.

Even so, eagles still face problems, including the lead poisoning that is common in eagles.

In a recent development, the turkey’s history with people goes back much further than Franklin. Scientists have found that turkeys were domesticated at least 1,500 years ago.

The information was obtained from Benjamin Franklin’s letter to Sarah Bache of January 26, 1784, as published by the National Archives in Founders Online from The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, the record of S.4610 on Congress.gov, and the enrolled text of the bill published by the U.S. Government Publishing Office.

Recent findings suggest that yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” claims Yin, of Cornell University.

Sources indicate that he applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin states, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin indicates.

Tech Report: The biggest concern about toddler screen time may be what children are missing

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many toddlers use screens daily, potentially missing valuable opportunities to play, talk, and learn through real human interaction.
  • At 18 months, children are learning to name things, put words together and make sense of the world around them.
  • In Hungary, researchers found that 49% of children around this age used screens every day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many toddlers use screens daily, potentially missing valuable opportunities to play, talk, and learn through real human interaction.

At 18 months, children are learning to name things, put words together and make sense of the world around them. Many are also becoming quite familiar with television and smartphones.

In Hungary, researchers found that 49% of children around this age used screens every day.

It has been revealed that there has been plenty of debate over how much screen time is appropriate for young children. A upcoming review, however, looks at a different side of the problem.

How much time is left for talking, playing and being with other people?

Krisztina Kopcsó, a researcher at the HCSO Institute for Quantitative Population and Economic Research in Budapest, led the review.

Kopcsó and her colleagues drew on data from a Hungarian national survey and research from around the world published since 2015.

Among the authors was Ákos Pogány from the Department of Ethology at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE).

“Young children learn primarily through actively exploring the world and interacting with others, rather than through screens. One of the greatest risks of introducing digital devices too early is that their use takes time away from precisely these essential experiences,” Pogány mentioned.

Screen exposure before age two is discouraged by the World Health Organization and the American Academy of Pediatrics. Video chatting with distant family members is treated as an exception.

Industry observers note that A more restrictive position has been adopted in France. Complete screen abstinence until age three was recommended by an expert committee appointed by the French President.

A recent Hungarian expert guideline also recommends avoiding screens before age three.

Despite these recommendations, early screen exposure is widespread. A 2022 meta-analysis included 63 studies and more than 89,000 children.

Only 24.7% of children under two were found to meet the guideline of no screen use.

In the United States, children under two averaged 63 minutes of screen media per day in 2024. These data were reported in the Common Sense Media census. By age two, 40% of children owned their own tablet.

Objective measurements were used in the Australian EUiLO cohort, described by Brushe and colleagues in 2023. A child-worn device recorded electronic noise for 16 hours on a typical day.

Recent findings suggest that families with lower educational attainment were oversampled among the 207 children. At 24 months, no screen exposure was recorded for only 2.4% of them.

Mean daily exposure in that cohort was 76.1 minutes at 6 months and 148.3 minutes at 24 months.

The Hungarian data were obtained from the Cohort ’18 Growing Up in Hungary panel study. A representative sample was recruited during pregnancy.

Sources indicate that maternal reports for 2,569 children were collected in 2019 and 2020 and analyzed by Kopcsó and colleagues in 2024. The children were aged between 15 and 23 months.

The database was weighted for maternal age, education, parity and marital status.

Daily screen exposure was reported for 49% of the children. More than one hour of exposure on a typical day was recorded for 37.5%. No exposure was reported for 14%.

Among daily customers, mean screen time on a typical day was 122.5 minutes.

Most children were cared for at home. Only 6.7% attended formal childcare at the time of the survey.

Television viewing was identified as the most frequent screen activity. It was watched every day by 43.6% of the children.

Videos on mobile devices were watched daily by 21.2% of children. Active touchscreen use on a daily basis was reported for 18.7%.

Higher screen time was observed in lower-income households and among children of less educated mothers. Both gradients were statistically significant in the 2024 analysis.

Sources indicate that A similar gradient was reported in a 2024 German study of 3,035 children by Paulus and colleagues. Parents there described using screens when time was short.

The contexts of screen use were also recorded in the Cohort ’18 survey.

Screen use while having fun with the child was reported by 62.1% of mothers.

According to recent reports, screens were allowed during household chores by 53.5%. Use for perceived developmental purposes was reported by 52.8%.

Background television was reported as a regular practice in 31.4% of families. It was rare or absent in 39.1%. The mother’s own relaxation was cited as a reason by 13.9%.

In Hungary, 19.6% of toddlers watched screens during meals, and 12.4% used them while falling asleep.

Children who spent more time with screens were read to and played with slightly less often, even after accounting for family income and mothers’ education.

However, busy parents may have less time for these activities, regardless of screen use.

A 2017 study linked screen use during more daily routines to delays in social and emotional development.

Another study in 2018 found that children who spent less time with screens at age two had better self-control at age four.

Apps and streaming content for babies are often marketed as educational.

A 2021 meta-analysis published in Child Development examined how well young children learn from videos compared with real-life demonstrations. Children aged 0 to 6 were included.

Less learning was found from video than from equivalent live demonstrations, and the gap narrowed with age.

Word learning from video was supported by adult co-viewing in a 2018 study by Strouse and colleagues.

Video chat was examined by Myers and colleagues in 2017 and by McClure and colleagues in 2018. Reciprocal interaction and joint attention cues are preserved in that format.

According to recent reports, screens were used to soothe or distract the child by 43% of Hungarian mothers. Frequent reliance on this strategy may reduce chances to practice self-regulation, the authors wrote.

Reciprocal associations between device use for calming and emotional reactivity were reported in a 2023 JAMA Pediatrics study.

Industry observers note that children aged 3 to 5 were followed. Similar associations were reported by Konok and colleagues at ELTE in 2024.

Autoplay, infinite scrolling and algorithmic recommendations are listed in the review as persuasive design features. Rapid cuts and high visual salience may also place heavy demands on immature attention.

According to recent reports, A parent’s phone can interrupt even the simplest moments with a child. In 2018, researchers McDaniel and Radesky used the term technoference to describe these interruptions.

Studies conducted in restaurants and public places in the United States and Israel found that parents paid less attention to their children while using phones.

Some even responded rather sharply when their children sought their attention.

A 2015 study found that just hearing a phone notification was enough to distract someone, even if they ignored it.

Babies seem to notice these interruptions, too. In a 2018 study, infants whose mothers frequently used phones had a harder time returning to a happy mood, even after their mothers put the devices away.

In the French ELFE cohort, mean daily screen time at age two was 49 minutes in 2013, among 12,099 children.

Television exposure during family meals at age two was associated with poorer expressive language.

Less advanced general cognitive development was found at age 3.5, Yang and colleagues reported in 2024. Overall screen time was not the factor identified.

Industry observers note that earth.com has previously covered how a parent’s own phone use relates to vocabulary growth. The role of eye contact in infant language learning has also been reported.

A harm-reduction approach to infant media use was proposed by Heller in Infant Behavior and Development in 2021.

Age-appropriate limits combined with harm-reduction strategies are recommended in the review.

Background and parallel media use during caregiving routines and play should be reduced. Screen exposure during meals and before bedtime should be avoided.

Caregiver co-use is prioritized when screens are introduced in the second or third year.

In a recent development, information could be provided to expecting parents through obstetric, prenatal and primary care services. Complaints about the no-screens-before-two rule have also been reported by parents.

Sources indicate that the European Union has rules to keep children safe online. Article 28 of its Digital Services Act focuses specifically on protecting young users.

On July 14, 2025, the European Commission also issued guidelines addressing features that could make it difficult for children to stop using digital platforms.

However, these measures do not specifically address the needs of babies and toddlers.

The authors argue that keeping children safe from the potential harms of digital media should not be the responsibility of parents alone.

Reducing screen time sounds like a sensible idea, but researchers still have much to learn about its benefits for very young children.

A 2025 review of experiments involving preschoolers found that programs teaching parents about screen habits helped reduce children’s screen use.

Industry observers note that few studies, however, have tested similar approaches in children under two. Even fewer have followed children long enough to see whether their language skills, sleep or ability to manage emotions improved.

Future studies could test whether replacing screen time with play and reading improves language development in children under two.

For young children, what they do after the screen goes off may be just as crucial as switching it off in the first place.

The review was published in the journal Biologia Futura.

#134577. A upcoming discovery could give the world 12 months to prepare for extreme El Niño and La Niña weather events

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1511 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

A upcoming discovery could give the world 12 months to prepare for extreme El Niño and La Niña weather events

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have found the conditions needed to predict some El Niño and La Niña events 12 months ahead of time.
  • Most El Niño forecasts are only reliable about six months ahead of time.
  • That is because the Pacific Ocean becomes so sensitive to tiny shifts in the spring that forecast models easily lose track of what comes next.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have found the conditions needed to predict some El Niño and La Niña events 12 months ahead of time.

Most El Niño forecasts are only reliable about six months ahead of time. Predicting a full year in advance has long been considered nearly impossible.

That is because the Pacific Ocean becomes so sensitive to tiny shifts in the spring that forecast models easily lose track of what comes next.

Now, researchers have found that certain 12-month El Niño forecasts really do hold up, depending on the state of the Pacific on the day the prediction is made.

Forecasts issued during a La Niña held up a year in advance in all nine climate models an Australian team tested. Forecasts issued when the Pacific was in neither phase did worse than a forecast built from nothing but the historical odds.

For farmers and water managers, that could mean months of extra warning before some El Niños.

Nandini Ramesh of CSIRO, Australia’s national science agency, and UNSW Sydney led the work. Her co-author Mandy Freund is at the University of Melbourne and the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century.

The team graded about 7,500 past forecasts rather than building a new forecasting system. Ramesh mentioned the researchers are still a few steps from applying the findings to agency models.

According to recent reports, in an interview with Earth.com, Freund noted the accuracy of forecasts that started during a La Niña surprised the team most. Routine checks of forecast performance, she said, often don’t sort forecasts by their starting state.

El Niño, La Niña and the neutral years between them make up a cycle scientists call the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO.

“Separating forecasts according to their starting state, we were able to uncover a much clearer picture of when long-range ENSO predictions can be trusted,” she stated.

Industry observers note that the warm phase of that cycle is El Niño, when the surface of the central and eastern tropical Pacific runs warmer than usual. La Niña is the cool phase. Both tend to peak around December, and both change weather patterns around the world.

Recent findings suggest that A declared El Niño or La Niña can set off drought warnings for farmers and water managers, the authors wrote. It can move the prices of farm commodities and start public health planning.

By one estimate they cite, seasonal forecasts influence companies worth a combined $13 trillion.

The trouble is the spring. From March to May the tropical Pacific is unusually sensitive to small disturbances. A forecast made before those months and aimed at the winter after them loses much of its skill.

Forecasters call this the spring predictability barrier. It is a massive part of why predictions beyond about nine months have stayed so difficult.

In a recent development, the team worked from an archive of decade-long climate simulations run by modeling centers in nine countries. Those include the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan and Canada.

These are physics-based models, which simulate the ocean and atmosphere from physical laws rather than past statistics.

The centers started a fresh batch every year from 1961 to around 2020, and the team used the runs that began between October and January.

Rather than judging the simulations on exact temperatures, the researchers asked one question of each: would the following winter land in La Niña, neutral or El Niño?

They sorted every year into one of those three bins using sea surface temperatures in a patch of the central Pacific. The coolest third of years counted as La Niña and the warmest third as El Niño.

Sources indicate that sorting the years that way left about 7,500 one-year forecasts to grade against NOAA‘s record of what the ocean actually did. Then the researchers split the results by which of the three states the Pacific was in when each forecast began.

In every one of the nine models, forecasts that began during a La Niña scored higher than forecasts that began during an El Niño or a neutral year.

Their skill a year out matched what seasonal forecast models manage three to four months ahead, a range forecasters already rely on.

Forecasts that began from a neutral Pacific did the opposite. In every model, they scored below a forecast built from nothing but the historical odds of one state following another.

Inside a single model, the gap between starting points was larger than the gap between the best and worst models.

“The finding that one-year forecasts starting from La Niña perform well in all nine of the models tested suggests there is something about La Niña conditions that makes the tropical Pacific system more predictable over the following year,” Freund said.

Stronger La Niña events were predicted better than weaker ones. For El Niño the pattern was less clear, though badly missed forecasts of strong El Niños were rare.

The team then asked the question a farmer might ask of any forecast: when a model predicts a particular switch, how often does it actually happen?

In one American model, a forecast of El Niño issued during a La Niña came true 82 percent of the time, a year ahead of the event. The same model’s forecast of a La Niña from neutral conditions came true only 9 percent of the time.

Recent findings suggest that three of the nine models were right more than 70 percent of the time when they predicted a La Niña would give way to an El Niño. Eight of the nine were at their worst predicting a La Niña from a neutral year, a switch that is rare in the real ocean.

Sources indicate that and when a model called for an El Niño from neutral conditions, not one beat the historical odds. Those calls are the likeliest false alarms.

Recent findings suggest that across all starts from neutral, the models were right 23 to 43 percent of the time. A forecast built from the historical odds alone would have been right 61 percent of the time.

Recent findings suggest that freund told Earth.com that the weakness from neutral starts remains an crucial caveat. “Unfortunately, starting from a neutral Pacific, the physics-based models often make the wrong predictions,” she mentioned.

“The system can be very sensitive: it is an example of what is known as the ‘butterfly effect’ where very small disturbances can be amplified over time into huge changes in a system’s behavior.”.

Asked by Earth.com what farmers and water managers should take from the result, Freund said the study is encouraging.

Industry observers note that those are people, she stated, who rely on knowing about an El Niño much further ahead than forecasts now allow. When a La Niña is under way, a forecast for the following year can be trusted more.

“This gives farmers, water managers and other decision-makers valuable extra time to prepare, including decisions about which crops and seed varieties to plant or how to manage water resources,” she said.

The method itself is simple, Freund said, and would not take much for forecasting agencies to consider. “It could provide this extra layer of confidence we can lay on certain predictions of ENSO,” she said.

The researchers also tested two-year forecasts, and for almost every kind of switch those were wrong more often than right.

In a recent development, the one exception came after an El Niño, when every model did better than the historical odds at saying there would be no El Niño for the next two years. Long stretches without an El Niño have been linked to multi-year droughts across the subtropics.

It has been revealed that why a La Niña makes the following year easier to predict is the open question. The team offered three possibilities.

According to recent reports, A La Niña’s cool water tends to linger into spring instead of fading in February or March the way an El Niño’s warmth does. Earlier studies also found fewer random atmospheric disturbances during a La Niña.

And a La Niña is when the upper tropical Pacific refills with warm water, so the state of that reservoir may carry a lot of information about what comes next.

The authors set aside long-term warming trends, slow decade-scale swings in the Pacific and the differences between one El Niño and another.

It has been revealed that they also didn’t test the statistical and machine learning methods they suspect would do better from a neutral start. Those methods work from past patterns instead of from today’s conditions. Whether the La Niña advantage holds in the models agencies actually run each season hasn’t been tested.

Industry observers note that the team’s next step is to work out which of the three explanations is doing the work. The confidence check it proposes can be run on any model from the forecasts it has already made.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

  • The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.
  • Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the newly introduced Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the newly introduced Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, stated Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

Recent findings suggest that “I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries stated on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”.

It has been revealed that departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

According to recent reports, it’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island mentioned in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of fresh well-paying union jobs.”.

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

Recent findings suggest that "We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., noted in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

According to recent reports, there’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the fresh Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”.

In a recent development, sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

A remote island in New Zealand was supposed to be a safe haven for wildlife

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A remote island off Newly introduced Zealand’s coast reveals the challenges of protecting native birds from invasive predators.
  • Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features Resolution Island, a remote expanse of wilderness off the southwestern coast of Fresh Zealand.
  • Surrounded by deep blue waters and covered in dense vegetation, the island appears to be an ideal sanctuary for wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A remote island off Newly introduced Zealand’s coast reveals the challenges of protecting native birds from invasive predators.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features Resolution Island, a remote expanse of wilderness off the southwestern coast of Fresh Zealand.

Surrounded by deep blue waters and covered in dense vegetation, the island appears to be an ideal sanctuary for wildlife.

Its isolation, however, has not always offered the protection that conservationists envisioned.

For more than a century, Resolution Island has been at the center of an ambitious effort to preserve some of Latest Zealand’s most extraordinary native birds.

Its history reveals both the potential and the limitations of using islands as natural barriers against invasive species.

The image was captured on December 12, 2025, by the Operational Land Imager aboard the Landsat 9 satellite.

Resolution Island lies within Fiordland National Park, a spectacular region of mountains, forests, waterfalls, and narrow waterways that extend deep into the southwestern coast of Newly introduced Zealand’s South Island.

During past ice ages, enormous glaciers moved through the region, gradually carving deep valleys into the landscape.

As the glaciers retreated and sea levels rose, ocean water flooded many of these valleys, creating the dramatic fjords visible today.

Resolution Island is the largest island within the national park. Its mountainous terrain reaches an elevation of 3,507 feet at the summit of Mount Clerke.

Recent findings suggest that the island’s varied landscape supports wetlands, ancient evergreen forests, and high-elevation grasslands. These distinct environments provide a range of habitats for native wildlife.

Fresh Zealand’s long geographical isolation allowed wildlife to evolve in remarkable ways.

Before humans arrived, the country had virtually no native land mammals other than bats. Birds occupied many ecological niches that mammals filled elsewhere in the world.

Some species gradually lost the ability to fly, while others developed behaviors that left them particularly vulnerable to ground-dwelling predators.

Among them were kiwi, which forage along the forest floor, and kākāpō, the world’s only flightless parrot.

For millions of years, these birds survived without facing the kinds of mammalian predators found on other continents.

That evolutionary advantage became a liability when people introduced unfamiliar animals into Upcoming Zealand’s ecosystems.

Rats, cats, and members of the weasel family brought latest pressures that native birds were poorly equipped to withstand.

By the nineteenth century, the decline of New Zealand’s native wildlife was becoming increasingly apparent.

European settlers had introduced stoats and other predators in an attempt to control rabbit populations. Instead, these animals created another ecological problem by preying on vulnerable native species.

In 1872, conservationist Thomas Henry Potts suggested that Resolution Island could provide a refuge for birds threatened by introduced predators.

The surrounding ocean appeared to offer a natural protective barrier, allowing native species to survive without the dangers they faced on the mainland.

Resolution Island became a protected reserve in 1891, making it part of a pioneering chapter in Newly introduced Zealand’s conservation history.

Long before modern wildlife restoration programs existed, naturalists were experimenting with ideas that would eventually become central to endangered species management.

One of the most dedicated figures in this undertaking was Richard Henry, who became the island’s caretaker.

Henry recognized the urgency of protecting birds that were rapidly disappearing from other parts of the country.

Working in an isolated and physically demanding environment, he transported hundreds of native birds across the waters of Fiordland.

More than 700 birds, primarily kiwi and kākāpō, were relocated to Resolution Island and neighboring islands during his conservation efforts.

Much of the work involved traveling by rowboat through a region known for challenging weather and rugged terrain.

Henry’s efforts represented an early attempt to prevent extinction by establishing wildlife populations in geographically isolated locations.

Unfortunately, the assumption that the surrounding waters would keep predators away proved incorrect.

According to recent reports, by 1900, invasive predators had been detected on Resolution Island. Stoats were capable of swimming across the channels that separated the island from nearby land.

The discovery undermined years of painstaking conservation work and exposed a weakness in the island’s natural defenses.

Industry observers note that stoats are highly adaptable hunters. Their ability to exploit different environments makes them particularly problematic in Fresh Zealand, where many native birds nest on or near the ground.

Henry attempted to control the invading predators through trapping but eventually left the island to pursue conservation work elsewhere.

His experience demonstrated that geographical isolation alone was not necessarily enough to protect vulnerable species.

More than a century later, conservationists continue to build on Henry’s original vision.

In 2008, Upcoming Zealand’s Department of Conservation rolled out a predator management program on Resolution Island to improve the prospects of native wildlife.

Maintaining such a program across a large, mountainous island presents considerable challenges.

Dense forests, steep slopes, and remote locations complicate efforts to monitor wildlife and control invasive animals.

Conservation also extends into the surrounding waters, where a marine reserve protects coastal ecosystems near the island’s distinctive Five Fingers Peninsula.

Viewed from space, Resolution Island offers a striking portrait of an apparently untouched wilderness.

Yet beneath its forest canopy lies a complex ecological history shaped by human intervention, invasive species, and generations of conservation work.

The island remains a powerful reminder that protecting nature sometimes requires far more than simply setting it aside.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/ Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

It has been revealed that “My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

#134571. Latest Update: What makes a hug truly memorable has a lot to do with empathy and how you handle relationships

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1125 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: What makes a hug truly memorable has a lot to do with empathy and how you handle relationships

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A survey of 15,049 adults shows most people remember hugs for comfort and support.
  • We tend to think of a hug as a universal source of warmth, yet nearly three in ten adults in a large survey could not recall one that had left a positive mark.
  • When a hug did stick in someone’s memory, it was much more likely to be for comfort, support, or understanding than for romance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A survey of 15,049 adults shows most people remember hugs for comfort and support. Empathy, attachment patterns, and hugging habits also play a role.

We tend to think of a hug as a universal source of warmth, yet nearly three in ten adults in a large survey could not recall one that had left a positive mark.

When a hug did stick in someone’s memory, it was much more likely to be for comfort, support, or understanding than for romance.

In a recent development, whether someone could remember a hug at all came down to a few key traits. The top three were how much empathy they felt, how they handled closeness, and whether they usually hugged their friends hello.

Recent findings suggest that anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol‘s School of Psychological Science led the analysis of 15,049 adults in the U.K. Their answers came from the Touch Test, a national survey on touch that BBC Radio 4 promoted in early 2020.

The study is a snapshot of who remembers what. It can show which traits go together with a hug memory, not what causes one.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dueren put the main finding simply. “Most participants remembered hugs because they conveyed comfort, understanding, or support,” she stated.

To her knowledge, she added, it’s the first large study to ask people why a hug stayed with them.

The question was plain: is there a hug you remember because of its positive emotional effect on you? Of the 15,046 people who answered, 10,457 stated yes, or 69.5 percent.

People who remarked yes then picked the single best reason from a short list. Among the 9,703 who chose a listed reason, about a third picked comfort, 29 percent said the hug conveyed understanding, and 20 percent said support.

According to recent reports, comfort, understanding, and support together cover more than four in five of the hugs people kept. Just 147 people, or 1.5 percent of the group, mentioned the hug was memorable because it was physically arousing.

Earlier studies had linked daily hugs to lower stress and better mood, and these answers fit.

Recent findings suggest that men and women were about equally likely to remember a hug at all. The reasons they gave, though, differed in a small but consistent way.

Among men, 3.9 percent chose arousal as the reason, compared with 0.8 percent of women. Men were also more likely to pick friendliness, 12.3 percent, in comparison to 4.8 percent of women.

Women chose comfort more often, at 34.6 percent to men’s 25.3 percent, and understanding more often too. The team suggested that the nurturing side of a hug may count for more among women.

Dueren’s team noted that only 2,197 men gave a reason, against 7,506 women, so they advise reading the gender differences with caution.

Dueren’s team, which includes researchers at UCL, the University of Sussex, and the University of Greenwich, then checked which traits went with keeping an emotional memory of a hug.

The strongest link was a habit: people who always greet friends and family with a hug were more likely to recall one.

Disliking the feel of being hugged went the other way, and so did finding it hard to know how firmly to hug someone. Asked by Earth.com what someone who dislikes hugging might take from the work, Dueren pointed to the size of the gap.

Industry observers note that “In our study, people who disliked the feeling of being hugged were slightly less likely to recall a hug that had a positive emotional effect on them than those who did not dislike it,” she said. “The findings highlight that hugging experiences are not equally remembered by everyone.”.

Empathy mattered too, whether measured as reading other people’s feelings or as feeling them alongside someone. Higher scores went with higher odds of remembering a hug.

So did attachment style, how a person relates to those closest to them. Insecure attachment comes in two forms.

Recent findings suggest that people who feel distress at separation, the anxious form, were more likely to hold a hug in memory. People who prize independence in relationships, the avoidant form, were less likely to.

All of these effects were small, and together the traits explained only 10 to 14 percent of the variation in who remembered a hug.

Recent findings suggest that dueren’s team expected that people who are less satisfied with their bodies would be more likely to remember a hug for the comfort or support it gave. That expectation failed.

Industry observers note that A person’s satisfaction with their own body did not influence whether they remembered a hug, or why. However, there was a measure that did.

In a recent development, the team built a five-item scale of how much a person’s sense of their body runs through touch. One item asked whether they choose clothes partly for how the fabric feels on the skin.

People who scored higher on it were more likely to remember a hug, and to remember it for understanding or arousal rather than comfort. The scale is new, and the team called those results preliminary.

According to recent reports, being tucked in with a hug and a kiss as a child had no bearing on whether a person remembered a hug. Neither did how often that person gets hugged day to day.

The people who answered chose to take part and were not paid, so they may care about touch more than average. Three-quarters were women, and all lived in the U.K., where attitudes to touch differ from those elsewhere.

The survey didn’t ask who gave the remembered hug or where it happened, so it can’t say whether comfort from a partner is remembered differently from comfort given by a friend.

In a recent development, answers were collected between January and March 2020, and fewer than 1 percent arrived after the U.K.’s first lockdown began. So this is a record of hugging before the pandemic changed it.

According to recent reports, dueren told Earth.com that she wants to pursue why the same hug feels so different to different people. “The same type of touch can feel pleasant for one person and uncomfortable to another,” she said. “I would like to better understand factors that contribute to these differences in experience.”.

In a recent development, empathetic people may store up hugs, or memorable hugs may make people more empathetic, and this survey can’t tell which. Settling that would mean following the same people over years, and that study has not yet been run.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a latest world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer indicates. “You have to really be curious.”.

In a recent development, minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

It has been revealed that minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

Industry observers note that minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

In a recent development, “I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a newly introduced person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

It has been revealed that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

Recent findings suggest that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., noted on Monday evening.

It has been revealed that asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”.

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

Industry observers note that “Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”.

Industry observers note that johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

In a recent development, also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”.

Kennedy noted Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”.

Sources indicate that “We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”.

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”.

In a recent development, but Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, noted she has seen such requests rolled out in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

In a recent development, and several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

Recent findings suggest that that includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”.

According to recent reports, republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott remarked. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”.

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

In a recent development, an online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

It has been revealed that sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”.

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”.

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” stated Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Sources indicate that cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”.

To help you find a STEM gift this holiday season that's both fun and educational, we’ve compiled a lineup of editor-approved robotics kits. In a recent development, during our research, we drew from our collective experience covering STEM toys and equipment for kids, including topics like the best microscopes and the best graphing calculators. We also read through studies on the importance of STEM education.

It has been revealed that while evaluating each kit, we gauged value for the price (especially because some kits cost upwards of $100), the STEM topics it covers, as well as how intuitive and (just as importantly) fun it is to use, according to parents’ reviews. Furthermore, we considered a wide variety of toys to account for different kids’ interests, ages, and skill levels.

According to recent reports, if you’re on the search for a robot kit with a variety of play options that isn't too expensive, this is it. The solar robot toy from Sillbird includes the pieces necessary to build 12 different robot designs, so your kid will never run out of newly introduced ways to play.

Sources indicate that the robotics kit offers two levels of difficulty, with half of the builds being simpler to assemble while the other half are more complex. So, once your kid masters the easier builds, they can move on to more challenging designs, all without ever needing a new toy.

It has been revealed that A unique feature of this robot in particular is its power source. Instead of burning through heaps of batteries like other robot toys, it relies exclusively on an integrated solar panel that sits on the robot’s head. Whenever it slows down, simply place it in some sunshine and wait for it to recharge.

It has been revealed that you can always count on Lego to be fun and engaging, but this kit throws in some coding and robotics to the classic building experience. This 1,177-piece set includes three Lego Star Wars droids—R2-D2, a Gonk Droid, and a Mouse Droid. Each of the droids looks like a standard Lego creation, but is designed to hold color and distance sensors, as well as an interactive motor.

Once they're built, kids can use the free Lego Boost smartphone app to program their droids and give them 40 different coding missions. Lego Boost is available on iOS, Android, Kindle, and Windows 10 devices.

With additional pieces included in the kit, kids can build and attach tools and weapons directly onto the droid for extra fun as they play.

This 77-piece activity set is reasonably priced and is perfect for beginners to coding and robotics. Botley the Coding Robot comes to life with an easy-to-use remote, so there are no apps to download (and no screen time involved). All coding is done directly on the remote control and Botley can be programmed to follow up to 120 steps in a row.

The kit includes coding activity sheets to help beginners learn the basics and get the most out of their robot. The kit also comes with several fun accessories, including black line pieces that Botley can follow on its own like a track, as well as several cubes and rods you can use to build obstacle courses.

For parents who want to introduce young kids to coding or build confidence in their fresh skills, Wonder Workshop’s Dash is a smart choice for young enthusiasts. Where many kits require extensive building before they’re up and running, Dash comes fully assembled and ready for about five hours of playtime before it needs a charge.

Each Dash is programmed to respond to external stimuli, so it can recognize and respond to dancing, singing, and the sound of your voice.

It has been revealed that this coding toy is compatible with Lego, allowing kids to use it as a base for making their own Lego creations. There are also five free apps to download that give kids fun coding project ideas, from beginner concepts to more advanced ones as they gradually get the hang of programming.

Makeblock’s mBot is an excellent toy for young programmers looking to challenge their knowledge and electronics skills in practical application. The small robot takes about 15 minutes to build using an easy-to-follow guide and step-by-step instructions in 3D.

Kids learn to code in Scratch, a graphic programming language, with free included software. There’s also an app with game-based tasks to challenge kids and help them advance their skills.

Recent findings suggest that the robot itself also has several features that expand its range of capabilities, such as the line follower sensor, the infrared sensor for the remote control, and the Bluetooth chip for controlling the bot from your phone. The toy is compatible with Lego bricks and has four expansion ports where you can add additional parts later on.

Sources indicate that there’s a lot to like about this very cute little robot ball. The Sphero also has built-in sensors that detect light, cardinal directions, gyroscopic direction, and speed.

In a recent development, what makes this robot special is how it allows owners to grow along with it. Once basic skills are mastered, young coders can move on to learning JavaScript, Scratch, and Swift.

Another plus is this robot toy’s durability. It’s waterproof and scratch-proof, so young explorers can take it outside through ponds and over rocks.

Robotics toys are, at their core, building toys. This kit from KiwiCo comes with internal motor pieces, external body parts, and blank robot skins so kids can design their own robot.

The finished product uses springs and a spinning mechanism to help the robot jump forward and rotate its arms. The key reason we like this kit so much is how well it focuses on hands-on application.

Unlike other options that are based in coding and higher-level thinking, this helps kids work with their hands and see how each individual piece interacts with the other.

Coding and basic electrical engineering are the focuses of this rover from Snap Circuits. Kids are challenged to build a full circuit board piece by piece, with over 30 parts to snap together, and then attach the board to the wheeled base.

Once the rover is built, kids code commands and directions for their “missions,” including patterns of flashing lights and sounds to get into the action.

One of the great things about this robot toy is that it takes kids from beginner to intermediate as their skills improve. After kids get a grasp of how to code through the app, they can create more advanced commands on their own using Blockly.

The robot also functions as a fun remote-control car that kids can drive in real time through the app.

This kit encourages kids to build and rebuild the robots, cars, and creatures of their dreams. It’s perfect for the budding inventor who likes to tinker with things around the house. There’s even a game element—10 playing cards that challenge kids to build various creations on the spot.

It has been revealed that protective goggles and a screwdriver accompany the included wooden pieces, electric motors and batteries, and hardware and tools. All the wooden pieces fit together easily and are designed with multiple purposes in mind.

While there is no coding element to the toy, its main focus is on helping kids build creative solutions to prompts and bolster their engineering and problem-solving skills.

Studies show that in addition to STEM literacy, robotics can help develop core skills like hands-on creativity, problem solving, communication, and teamwork. So teaching robotics isn’t just about setting up your kid to have a career as a computer programmer or engineer—it equips them with tech know-how and critical thinking they’ll need for virtually any type of education or work.

Recent findings suggest that choose toys that allow your kid to use their imagination and play out multiple different situations, both real and made up. Furthermore, make sure even if you want the toy to help them learn STEM skills, it still fits their interests and passions. A toy that gets played with often will help them learn a lot more than a more educational one that collects dust.

While you may think robotics clubs are only for middle and high schoolers, research has shown that children are also able to master basic robotics and programming skills when they’re introduced in pre-K to second grade.

Many of these kits are appropriate for children as young as 3 years old, while some are more advanced with an age suggestion of 8 and up. Before you buy, check the recommended age range listed by the firm or on the box to make sure you’re choosing a robotics kit that challenges your kid while still being accessible to them.

Sources indicate that you don’t have to shell out hundreds of dollars right away on a robot, especially if your kids are still learning what they like. There are plenty of robotics kits that run under $50 if you aren’t sure your kids are going to enjoy this kind of play and learning. Pricier options over $100 offer more complexity and can often grow with the kids, since they’re customizable to continue challenging them as they get older and gain experience.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

According to recent reports, to piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Sources indicate that most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo notes. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

Sources indicate that I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Sources indicate that brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Recent findings suggest that republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Industry observers note that republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.
  • Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Industry observers note that challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Industry observers note that he and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and promptly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

According to recent reports, how explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

In a recent development, that tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern notes. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a newly introduced version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”.

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these fresh ideas, Stern indicates. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

In 1985, the W.M. Keck Foundation donated $70 million for the University of California and Caltech to construct a newly introduced observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The twin telescopes of the Keck Observatory would be larger than any previous telescope, and the first to use a segmented-mirror design. The goal was a facility that could see farther out into the universe, and with more detail, to study exoplanets, black holes, star and planet formation, and more.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 24, 1990, with only nine of the 36 segments of its mirror in place, Keck I turned skyward and achieved first light. The telescope’s image of NGC 1232 was an auspicious beginning of a long career for the Keck Observatory, furthered when Keck I was completed in 1992, and when Keck II was constructed and saw first light in October 1996. The twin telescopes would become the most scientifically productive optical and infrared telescopes in the world.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.
