Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1385 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming new stars.
  • According to recent reports, but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict.
  • Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming new stars. These so-called quiescent galaxies have lived for billions of years and over that time, gradually exhausted their star-forming gas. By contrast, galaxies that lie at much greater distances — and thus appear to us when they were young, in the early universe — should have plenty of gas and be readily forming stars.

According to recent reports, but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict. Astronomers don’t know why they have stopped forming stars so soon, but they have many theories. Some of them require dark energy to have had a stronger influence in the early universe than previously thought, and thus have profound impacts on our understanding of the universe and its evolution.

Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born. This could explain the high number of young but unexpectedly quiescent galaxies JWST has found without needing drastic changes to our understanding of dark energy and its influence over time.

Recent findings suggest that in order to form stars, galaxies need reservoirs of gas that are dense and cold, lacking energy and prone to collapsing inward. One way to end a galaxy’s era of star formation — a process that astronomers call quenching — is to trigger strong winds that blast outward from the galaxy. These vast, high-speed flows of charged particles can blow away or heat this cold gas.

Such galactic winds can have two possible sources of energy. One is an actively accreting central supermassive black hole (called an active galactic nucleus, or AGN). The other is the energetic blasts generated by massive stars that form and then quickly die, ending their lives by exploding as supernovae. But astronomers have never caught such a wind in the act of draining its host of gas in the early universe, as it is difficult to get a detailed look inside a galaxy so far away.

To better discern the inner workings of star-forming galaxies in the early universe, researchers carried out a joint survey combining observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) — a powerful radio observatory in Chile — and infrared data from JWST. They also turned to archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope. A team led by astrophysicist Rebecca Davies of Swinburne University of Technology in Australia spotted one particular galaxy, called CRISTAL-02, that indicates what appears to be the first direct evidence of a wind powerful enough to halt star formation in a massive galaxy just 1.1 billion years after the Massive Bang. The discovery was published June 10 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

Sources indicate that CRISTAL-02 is part of a larger sample of around two dozen star-forming galaxies at a similar distance (and therefore of a similar age). Observations revealed a huge plume of cold gas extending outside the galaxy, almost as large as the galaxy it comes from. The plume is moving toward Earth at some 60 miles (100 kilometers) per second. Finding fast-moving gas so far from the galaxy is a sign the gas is being actively pushed out in a wind-driven process.

According to recent reports, but to truly determine the nature of the plume, the team first had to rule out another possibility behind its formation: Because CRISTAL-02 also appears to be in the throes of merging with several other galaxies, the plume could be a tidal tail — gas stripped away by gravitational forces during the interaction, rather than a genuine wind. This was tricky to determine, Davies claims, as no single measurement could settle the question of the gas’ origin; instead the team had to combine several different measurements to characterize the plume and confirm its cause.

First, Davies’ team measured how many fresh stars the galaxy produces each year. Massive stars live much shorter lives than less massive ones, so looking at how many young, massive stars are in a galaxy indicates how quickly it is forming new stars to replace the ones that are dying. So, the team searched for signs of these young, massive stars in the galaxy’s spectrum and measured how bright those features appear.

It has been revealed that the researchers also needed to determine how much gas the galaxy is losing. They did so by first using ALMA data to calculate the mass in the plume and then combining it with the gas’ velocity and distance from the galaxy’s center.

Sources indicate that the verdict: CRISTAL-02 is forming stars at roughly three times the rate of a typical galaxy its size at this distance, but is losing twice as much gas as the galaxy’s star-formation rate. “If this rapid blowout continues, the galaxy could be dead in less than 50 million years, explaining the origin of the mysterious massive dead galaxies in the early universe,” Davies said in a press release.

Finally, the team turned to identifying the cause of the plume. Was the gas being pushed out by energy coming from the galaxy’s central black hole, or was the galaxy’s burst of intense star formation — and the resulting supernova blasts — the culprit?

Recent findings suggest that models predict that the most powerful outflows from massive galaxies like these should be the result of accretion onto supermassive black holes, Davies says. But CRISTAL-02 shows no sign of AGN activity in its center. On the other hand, based on the amount of massive young stars in the galaxy, Davies’ team calculated that the energy transferred to the surrounding gas as these stars die and explode as supernovae would be powerful enough to produce the observed plume.

The speed of the gas backs this idea up. Supernova-driven outflows rarely exceed speeds of about 1,550 miles (2,500 km) per second, indicates Christy Tremonti, an astronomer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the study. Velocities higher than this usually point to an AGN as the energy source. CRISTAL-02’s outflow is moving around 400 miles (640 km) per second, comfortably within the range expected for a wind produced by a powerful starburst.

Davies says that “the result is surprising,” going against the conventional wisdom that AGN are the cause of star-formation-ending winds. Tremonti notes that  “theoretical models love to use AGN feedback to shut off star formation in massive galaxies — almost every simulation does.” Yet CRISTAL-02’s star formation alone appears capable of triggering a wind that could exhaust its gas supply within tens of millions of years.

In a recent development, CRISTAL-02’s story may not be an isolated case, Davies says. Studies suggest that around 40% of massive star-forming galaxies in the early universe are merging, meaning many of them may be caught in similar growth spurts. If this commonly results in subsequent supernova-driven winds, it could help explain why so many early galaxies burned brightly and died young. “It may be the case that AGN are really important for keeping star formation off, but maybe they’re not the thing that shuts it down initially,” Tremonti says.

It has been revealed that the case isn’t entirely closed. Davies says her team cannot completely rule out the presence of an active supermassive black hole — either one too faint to detect, or one that may have flared briefly in the past and pushed gas away from the galaxy before subsequently fading from view. Tremonti agrees this is one of the hardest scenarios to eliminate. Future observations in the mid-infrared, which can peer through dust that might otherwise hide a buried black hole, could help close this gap.

As for CRISTAL-02, its fate is somewhat ironic: The explosive burst of star formation it is undergoing is also the underlying cause of its imminent death.

It has been revealed that shreejaya Karantha is a science writer based in India. Her work has appeared in Sky & Telescope, Phys.org, Live Science US, and The Hindu.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that even the best-laid aims can require a bit of luck to execute.
  • “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy.
  • The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that even the best-laid aims can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

“I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

Industry observers note that he named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

“There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” claims Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”.

It has been revealed that mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Massive Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the glitch near and dear to his heart: health care.

In a recent development, “Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the glitch,” Coss notes. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Industry observers note that romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

It has been revealed that beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me latest appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss claims. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much. Power stations are handy, but once they run out of power, they take a long time to recharge. That’s where a smaller-sized portable generator can really shine. So long as you have the fuel, they can keep running.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few notable things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type. For portable power, models that output 2,000 to 5,000 watts will generally be simple enough to lift in and out of a truck, though some models that generate more are designed to be lightweight. Anything over 100 pounds starts to buck the idea of something being portable, even if it has wheels.

In a recent development, fuel type matters, too. All generators run on gas, but dual-fuel models can also run on propane. The drawback is that propane delivers slightly less power output and shorter running time, but it runs a lot cleaner and is much less messy to deal with.

In a recent development, if you’re powering sensitive electronics like digital equipment or TVs, you’ll also want to look for an inverter generator, which delivers more stable “cleaner” power that won’t damage your gear. They also run quieter than standard models. For these reasons, all of the picks on our list are inverter generators.

Sources indicate that keeping portability in mind, the models we cover in this story are all 7,500 watts and under. For the models that we tested, we based our methods on our experience using generators for backup power with and without transfer switches, on construction sites to run power tools and equipment, as well as running sound systems and lighting at outdoor events. We measured the sound levels of these generators idling with no load, and while running under load at two feet and 25 feet. We then used an oscilloscope to observe the sine wave of the alternating current generated by these machines, and a clamp meter to check voltage output.

Recent findings suggest that some examples of devices we used with large starting and running loads include a large air conditioner and a portable table saw. In one case, we even tested it paired to a solar inverter-charger. We evaluated these generators based on ease of starting, power response, sound levels, value, safety, and reliability to select the top performers.

It has been revealed that the Honda EU2200i inverter generator has just about everything you want from a portable generator. It’s half the size and weight of comparable generators in its class; it’s very quiet and clean when operating; and it’s fully enclosed so you can swiftly and easily transport it and move it around without worrying about it getting caught on anything.

That enclosure is an vital feature, as it protects the inverter electronics and helps contain noise—the EU2200i is remarkably quiet. In testing, we measured sound levels of 68.9 decibels at the generator under no load. When we switched it to “eco” mode, which reduces engine speed when power isn’t called for, the sound was reduced to 76 decibels.

In a recent development, when we used an oscilloscope to look at the sine wave of the current generated, the curves were smooth and symmetrical, an indicator of “clean” power. This remained true even when running heavy loads from devices like a table saw or an air conditioner.

Recent findings suggest that there are some nice design features, too. The vent on the gas cap closes so fumes or fuel cannot escape. You could breathe freely packing this in the passenger compartment of an SUV. Likewise, the power on/off switch doubles as a fuel shutoff, so it can’t be forgotten.

Sources indicate that lastly, the EU2200i has ports for parallel operation. With the correct cable kit, it connects to a second EU2200i to double the output to 4,400 starting and 3,600 running watts. The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on.

In a recent development, we like the GD400BN because it’s powerful, quiet, and portable at a reasonable price point. The interesting thing about this inverter generator is how much power it can deliver, yet it’s still as compact as similar generators that deliver half as much output. Even when running on lower-output propane as the fuel source, it can run up to 3,000 watts, which is considerable for a generator that only weighs 47 pounds.

Industry observers note that another plug or two would’ve been nice, however. Its single AC outlet limits you to plugging one power tool or appliance at a time, despite having enough output to power more than one device. It does have a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet for connecting to an RV, though, so that does make up for it a bit, but only if you have that need. The 1.1-gallon fuel tank is also a bit limiting regarding runtime for gasoline, but that’s easily overcome by using propane. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator, and at a list price of $600, it comes at a reasonable price to boot.

The Wen DF360iX offers a considerable amount of utility for an affordable price. You have the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane with a running output of up to 2,900 watts. While propane delivers a bit less at 2,600 watts, that’s plenty of power for a job site or camping use and even enough electricity for small to midsize RVs.

While this generator is fairly light at 49 pounds, it doesn’t cut back on ports, including a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV. There are also two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise at a quarter load, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t bother the neighbors. There are some nice safety features, too, including auto-shutoff if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present.

It has been revealed that of course, with any generator in this price range (under $500), there are compromises. This model has a pretty small fuel tank—only 1.5 gallons—so you won’t be able to run this on gasoline for long periods (around five hours with a half-load) without having to stop and refill. You can mitigate this, however, by relying on a larger tank of propane. For example, a 20-pound tank should enable you to run it for up to 14 hours.

GENERATOR SAFETYWhile not hard to run, generators present dangers, so you need to follow basic safety rules. Never operate them in a closed space, like a garage or shed. Exhaust gases contain carbon monoxide (CO), a lethal, odorless, colorless gas. Most manufacturers offer models that shut down when they detect carbon monoxide building up. Do not run a generator in a garage with the door open, or in front of the garage with the door open, because carbon monoxide can still get trapped and seep into the house. Run generators at least 20 feet away, including from windows and doors, with the exhaust blowing away from the house.

Industry observers note that RV owners need a generator outfitted with at least a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet, but it also helps to have a decent amount of power to go with it, so that you can run things like a heater or an air conditioner. This model from Champion offers both, with the outlet and up to 3,500 running watts, which is enough to power a small- to medium-sized RV.

It has been revealed that it also offers great fuel flexibility. With a full 2.3-gallon fuel tank, it should be able to run for up to 14 hours, but it’s dual-fuel, so with a full 20-pound propane tank, this generator can supply 21 hours of uninterrupted power.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to being a solid companion for camping and RVing, this generator could serve as a useful tool in an emergency at home where power is needed. Using a manual transfer switch, you could power a few 120-volt circuits using the 30-amp connection. And the inverter will help to keep it running more quietly, which is helpful at home or the campground.

It has been revealed that one of our test editors picked up this generator when faced with a home emergency where he needed a generator with specific features, quickly, and on a budget. A failed generator at a solar-powered off-grid cabin necessitated the quick acquisition, and, happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator highlighted up on the doorstep in only two days.

In about 15 minutes, with minimal assembly and after adding oil, the generator was connected to a propane cylinder by a hose and was running on the first cycle of the starter. Since then, it’s run steadily at 500 watts, up to 5,500 watts, at 240 volts (great for powering high-voltage appliances like dryers or water pumps), to charge a battery bank during the winter when sunlight wasn’t enough to get the job done.

This Pulsar puts out very clean power, too, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger it was paired with.

Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features.

Generac’s iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator is a great example of what we love about dual-fuel, inverter generators. This type of generator can deliver cleaner power than a standard model, meaning there’s less distortion in the electrical current frequency. That’s ideal for powering sensitive electronics, such as TVs, computer equipment, and smart household appliances. This is also a closed-frame inverter generator, which tends to be quieter; the iQ3800 is one of the quietest generators we’ve tested of this size.

Recent findings suggest that we were very impressed with how easy the iQ3800 is to operate. The electric start and auto choke worked perfectly, taking only about four to five seconds, while the manual pull-start also fired up the generator with minimal effort. Switching between fuel types was also very simple to perform. Once running, you can view vital information on an easy-to-read LED display that lists the total hours the machine has run, the fuel level for the gasoline tank (there’s no gauge for propane), and a load gauge that uses a bar graph to show power output level—knowing that helps to avoid overloading the generator.

The inverter technology might be the most crucial feature of the iQ3800. This generator has a total harmonic distortion (THD)—a level of variance in the current frequency—of less than 3 percent, which is very low. Essentially, anything with a screen or any smart device would be best powered using an inverter generator like the iQ3800. It’s an ideal generator to power RVs in campgrounds or off-grid, and a great option for emergency backup in urban areas.

Full Generac iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator Review.

These generators, sometimes called backup generators, are used to provide temporary power when and where it is needed. Portable is a relative term; some are more portable than others. While the smallest models can be picked up and carried, most have wheels and a handle to make transport easier. However, at 100 pounds or more, picking them up to load or move may take two people. Appliances, power tools, or other devices can be plugged directly into standard outlets on the generator’s front panel.

Additionally, many models have a twist-lock plug that can provide up to 240 volts and be used to power circuits in a home via a manual transfer switch. You may hear generators like these referred to as “open frame” generators, which simply means that the engine, fuel tank, and generator components are not enclosed in bodywork.

Though inverter-type generators are—like their standard cousins—typically portable, we group them separately because they’re significantly and technically different in terms of how they work.

Like most generators, inverter generators provide 120/240 volts of AC power. They generate AC current just like the others, but it’s then converted to DC (Direct Current), and then inverted back to AC. The conversion and inversion is controlled by circuitry which acts like a filter, flattens surges, and cleans up the sine wave (or oscillating wave) of the electrical current.

Typical generators have varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current. This isn’t usually an concern for most electrical devices, though sensitive electronics like tablets, laptops, televisions, and other smart devices can be damaged by current distortion or surges. These devices will last longer with “clean” power and steady voltage. Because of that added complication, inverter generators can be significantly more expensive.

In a recent development, standby generators are permanently installed and connected to a home. These may power selected, critical circuits during a power outage, or may provide power for the whole home. Standby generators have systems that monitor power supplied by a utility and start automatically in the event of an outage. Since they’re not portable or easily moved, we didn’t include any here.

It’s important to know what you intend to power with a generator in order to choose the right size. Manufacturers list two figures for generators: starting watts and running watts. Starting watts include the initial surge required to start appliances or tools with powerful electric motors or compressors. Once started, these devices require far less power to run continuously.

Many manufacturers have a chart with estimated power requirements for common appliances and tools to help you figure out what you need. For a more precise measurement, you can also calculate the figure yourself by adding up the power consumption of specific appliances and adding them together.

According to recent reports, to calculate watts, multiply voltage (usually 120 volts) by the amps (amperage) required to run the appliance (usually found on a tag attached to the appliance). Do this for each item that the generator will power.

Most portable generators are powered by gasoline, the most commonly available fuel. However, when using generators for emergency power, their infrequent use presents some problems to consider.

The first is that when major, catastrophic storms hit and power outages last for days, gas stations may struggle to meet demand, resulting in long lines. The second glitch has to do with the infrequent use of backup generators, which may sit for months to years between uses.

Gasoline sitting in a carburetor will slowly evaporate over time, leaving gummy deposits that can block fuel from getting through, making it difficult or even impossible to start your generator without servicing. You can avoid this by closing the fuel valve and letting the generator run until it stalls, using up the remaining fuel in the carburetor. Also, over time, gasoline can oxidize or become “stale,” losing combustibility. It may also absorb water, which can then corrode fuel tanks and other metal components in the fuel system. Starting a generator regularly, as well as treating fuel with a stabilizer, can help fight these issues.

Ethanol-free gasoline, available at some gas stations, is also less susceptible to degradation over time than standard 87-octane pump gas; however, it’s still a good idea to mix the fuel going into your generator with stabilizer.

Dual-fuel generators can run on gasoline or liquified petroleum gas (LPG), commonly known as propane. Switching between the fuels is simple, and you won’t be tied to the availability of one type of fuel.

A massive advantage of propane is that it’s very stable when stored for long periods of time. It won’t go stale, and it won’t gum up carburetors from sitting. Plus, some homes that use propane for other purposes may already have large storage tanks on the premises, foregoing the need to make repeated trips out for fuel.

In a recent development, the downside to propane is that it creates fewer BTUs (British Thermal Units, a measurement of energy) than the same amount of gasoline. So, a generator running on propane will have slightly reduced starting and running watts. On the plus side, though, it will also run a little quieter than those that run on gasoline.

Sources indicate that while not as common, tri-fuel generators add an option to connect by natural gas. Some propane-powered generators can be converted to run on natural gas, as well. Like propane, natural gas can run cleaner and a little quieter. However, it also creates fewer BTUs than gasoline and propane, so it will also produce reduced starting and running watts.

Natural gas also requires a dedicated line for the generator, which most homes that have access to natural gas will not have, and thus will need to be professionally installed.

If you’re powering appliances, tools, or other devices by plugging them directly into the standard outlets on the generator, the answer is no. If the generator is being used to power circuits in your home, maybe. It’s always best to consult the operator’s manual, a licensed electrician, or your local building officials about township ordinances—some localities may have requirements that differ from the National Electrical Code (NEC).

Electrical circuits need to be grounded to operate devices safely, so that any current that shorts out or has a fault is directed to the ground, i.e., the actual, literal earth, so the user doesn’t become the conduit to “ground.”.

Industry observers note that there are two ways that generators are grounded: neutral-bonded and floating neutral. Neutral-bonded means the neutral wire is connected (i.e., bonded) to the generator frame. With a floating neutral, the neutral is not connected to the frame. In the latter case, the generator should be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a grounding rod driven into the ground.

According to recent reports, generators with ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlets, when used to power circuits in your home, require neutral switching and a manual transfer switch, and must be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a ground rod driven into the soil. Neutral-switching transfer switches are also referred to as three-pole transfer switches.

There could be numerous reasons for difficulty starting a generator. The first things to check are whether or not there's any fuel in the tank, and if the fuel valve is turned open. Then, check for any obstructions in the air cleaner box. If that’s clean, move on to check that the engine has spark.

If your generator has sat for a long time without treated fuel, the carburetor may be clogged up and require cleaning—if you’re unfamiliar with any of these steps, it may be best to take it to a shop for service.

In an emergency, use what you can get, but as a general rule, 87 octane fuel will be fine—just don’t go lower than that.

In a recent development, as long as we’re talking fuel, it’s always best to use ethanol-free fuel in equipment with small gas engines—if that’s not possible, nothing more than 10-percent ethanol. Ethanol can attract moisture, which will then separate and settle in the gas tank or carburetor, where it can corrode and clog the fuel system. For this reason, it’s also a good idea to treat gas with a fuel stabilizer.

Sources indicate that much like your lawn mower, generators need regular maintenance. However, since they often see less use, maintenance intervals tend to be farther apart. Typical maintenance would include changing oil, checking the air filter and changing it if needed, changing the fuel filter if so equipped, and checking the spark plug.

The best source of specific maintenance and troubleshooting information for your generator is the owner’s manual.

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 24: A Super Beaver Moon occults the Pleiades.

The distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

In a recent development, although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?
  • As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for fresh member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.

Trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s latest member orientation. Giddy, even.

The incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

“I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” said Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

It has been revealed that forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

It has been revealed that “I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he mentioned of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”.

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” stated Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

According to recent reports, cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

“The congressman said that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s crucial that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

“This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke stated. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”.

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

“I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” said Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

But just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” stated Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

According to recent reports, “I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he mentioned.

After arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander remarked he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he remarked.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”.

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he said.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their newly introduced workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” mentioned Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

“They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander noted.

Industry observers note that born in Macon, France, on Nov. 25, 1783, Claude-Louis Mathieu highlighted an aptitude for mathematics from a young age. Despite his family’s poverty and his father’s wish for him to be a carpenter, Mathieu moved to Paris in 1801 to study for admission to the prestigious Ecole Polytechnique. He became a student at Ecole Polytechnique two years later and graduated from the school in 1805.

A varied career in astronomy followed, during which Mathieu served as secretary, assistant to the director, and later astronomer at the Paris Observatory, conducting research focused on calculating stars’ parallaxes and determining stellar distances. He also became a professor of astronomy at the College de France, a writer and editor, and a driving force behind the adoption of the metric system in France. Mathieu was elected president of the International Metre Commission in 1870 although he was in his late 80s, and continued to work in that position into his 90s.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

It has been revealed that maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

According to recent reports, house Republicans had hoped that latest congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” noted Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the fresh lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

New maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, said he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

According to recent reports, advocates for a latest map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley remarked he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

It has been revealed that republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in New York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for newly introduced maps in 2028.

According to recent reports, officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

Recent findings suggest that it’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass fresh maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where latest maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, mentioned last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In Fresh Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Industry observers note that democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their new majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to newly introduced maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity.
  • For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

It has been revealed that but giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” states Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

It has been revealed that what traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Industry observers note that those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health concerns — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

That thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”.

Sources indicate that the higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”.

It has been revealed that yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Sources indicate that englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

According to recent reports, the ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

Sources indicate that he and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

But the study also indicated that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

In a recent development, then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their latest masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work shows. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”.

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott states. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”.

In a recent development, most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he states. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”.

Recent findings suggest that fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”.

In a recent development, perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales right now in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Sources indicate that below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

Movember Institute of Men’s Health.

It has been revealed that all the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Sources indicate that fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he says.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”.

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, claims psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a new masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”.

Sources indicate that such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher indicates. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis states. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

According to recent reports, however the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis notes. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”.
