The 7 Best Portable Jump Starters to Bring Your Vehicle Back to Life

📅 23 Nov 2021 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • If you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help.
  • A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

In a recent development, like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also important to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

Recent findings suggest that there are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In short, each device in this roundup can rapidly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

Recent findings suggest that my recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

According to recent reports, with 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

Industry observers note that this device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts.

Recent findings suggest that the GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—notable so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an concern.

Recent findings suggest that protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

In a recent development, the interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review.

This is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

In a recent development, it has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

According to recent reports, like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Industry observers note that its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

In a recent development, the Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

Full Noco GB40 Boost Plus Review.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.).

Industry observers note that I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so owners need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

In a recent development, the Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

Recent findings suggest that for motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

This device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

In a recent development, with 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

In a recent development, for years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

With 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

This portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Recent findings suggest that something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

The Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

According to recent reports, portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

It has been revealed that the two most notable specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

According to recent reports, bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

Most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

It has been revealed that if you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

Look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

Yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Industry observers note that peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two vital. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

According to recent reports, definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will issue a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

Yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against problems like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That mentioned, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov.
  • Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.
  • The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

According to recent reports, colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

Recent findings suggest that with his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

Sources indicate that that majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Recent findings suggest that republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

According to recent reports, colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

It has been revealed that “I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I mentioned, ‘You got to run,’” the Newly introduced York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” notes a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

Sources indicate that major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

In a recent development, the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

Latest Update: The 7 Best Pocket Knives for Everyday Tasks and Outdoor Adventures

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Cutting tools were likely some of the earliest tools fashioned by our prehistoric ancestors, so it’s perhaps surprising that knives are still one of the most popular tools in an age of 3D printers and electric scooters.
  • Modern EDC pocket knives have evolved quite a way beyond stone shards, with a bewildering variety of blade steels, blade shapes, opening and locking mechanisms as well as diverse aesthetics ranging from tactical to minimalist to outdoorsy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Cutting tools were likely some of the earliest tools fashioned by our prehistoric ancestors, so it’s perhaps surprising that knives are still one of the most popular tools in an age of 3D printers and electric scooters.

Modern EDC pocket knives have evolved quite a way beyond stone shards, with a bewildering variety of blade steels, blade shapes, opening and locking mechanisms as well as diverse aesthetics ranging from tactical to minimalist to outdoorsy.

This guide focuses on functional folding knives with (mostly) approachable price tags that you’ll want to use every day, not place under glass. I test dozens of knives each year, and I’ve chosen my favorites below only from the knives I’ve personally used.

According to recent reports, the Iridium is one of Kershaw’s most popular releases and for good reason. It’s priced modestly with a secure bar lock-out, easy one-handed opening and closing, and it just looks cool. It’s also the sweet spot for most people in terms of size, weight, and style. Not ultralight (just over three ounces), the 6061-T6’s aluminum handle and slim profile keep it barely noticeable in your pocket.

In a recent development, when testing, I found the 4.5-inch length was great for my medium-sized hands and shouldn’t be too big or small for any hands—or jobs. Kershaw offers low- and mid-priced production knives made in China, but they follow up with high-quality control in their Oregon facilities and consistently deliver designs that just work.

At the core of the Iridium series is a secure, Benchmade-style crossbar lock, and while there are models that veer into Benchmade prices, many models, including the original, can be had for less than $100.

Sources indicate that the Iridium is easy to use—opening with a smooth action, activated by the thumb stud opener. Though it’s not spring-assisted, the blade flicks open fast without resistance. Closing is similarly smooth—just pull down on the crossbar lock and close with a finger, or hold upright and let the blade fall shut. I usually prefer the satisfying speed of a flipper, but the smooth action of the Iridium’s thumb stud opening rivals the Benchmade Bugout’s, and it quickly grew on me.

Sources indicate that the D2 steel used in the original, which offers decent edge retention and durability, is common in lower-cost knives but can rust if you abuse it. A compromise option: Go with the black oxide-coated D2 blade which keeps all but the cutting edge sealed off from rust. The look on all these versions of the Iridium matches the modern design features, and the only drawback of how smooth and slick the knife looks is that it’s not the best for operating in wet or muddy conditions where grip could become an issue.

Full Kershaw Iridium Pocket Knife Review.

Coast is one of several Oregon-based knife manufacturers (the organization also sells a wide range of flashlights and headlamps) to offer a range of budget-friendly folding pocket knives. My favorite from their lineup is the fairly small but robust Contra, which has an all-metal build and a lifetime warranty despite the low cost. The wharncliffe blade, made from a softer 7CR17 steel, dulls faster than high-end steels but has the benefit of being easy to sharpen at home.

Sources indicate that the wharncliffe blade gives you the utility of a box cutter blade but much more versatility as you retain a decent point for puncturing tasks, and I’ve come to prefer it for everyday carry over more traditional drop point shapes. Coast adds durability to its budget steel with a black oxide coating that I found doesn’t scratch easily. The knife is a full stainless-steel build with a good-looking stonewash finish on the handle which integrates the frame lock system.

Recent findings suggest that the flipper opening is fast and satisfying for knife fidgeters but it’s usually safer to employ a two-handed closure. Given the overseas production and ultra-low sticker price, this pocket knife’s durability could be a potential concern, but I’ve used mine roughly near-daily for more than a year and haven’t broken or chipped the blade. It still looks fresh.

Benchmade is an American knife brand based in Oregon with a loyal following for its premium production pocket knives. Known for lightweight designs, modern materials, and innovation, the brand has produced many favorites—but my top pick is the Benchmade 535 Bugout.

To me, the Bugout captures what Benchmade does best: an ultralight folder that’s still strong, well-built, and made with high-quality steel (and the same holds true with the Benchmade 533 Mini Bugout). Some might argue the Benchmade Osborne 940 is the brand’s most iconic knife, but I reach for the Bugout every time—especially for hunting, camping, backpacking, or backcountry skiing, where weight matters.

Industry observers note that the design is modern without feeling overly tactical. It’s streamlined with a simple profile and a practical drop-point blade. The textured Grivory scales—glass-reinforced plastic—keep weight incredibly low while maintaining rigidity.

Sources indicate that at under two ounces and just 0.42 inches thick, the Bugout is barely noticeable in a pocket, making it ideal for long outdoor trips. For those who don’t like the Grivory feel, there are versions with aluminum or carbon-fiber scales and a range of steel options.

Operation is another highlight. Benchmade’s Axis Lock uses a spring-loaded crossbar that allows easy one-handed opening and closing from either hand while keeping fingers out of the blade path. The mechanism is simple, strong, and easy to maintain—I even built one myself at the Benchmade factory and found it intuitive without instructions.

Sources indicate that in terms of cutting performance, my Bugouts arrived razor-sharp out of the box. I prefer the standard S30V steel because it balances edge retention with easier sharpening in the field, though higher-end options like S90V are available if you want longer-lasting sharpness. S30V is also tough and corrosion-resistant, which suits hard outdoor use.

It has been revealed that benchmade’s lifetime warranty and sharpening service add real long-term value. The Bugout isn’t cheap, but with its reliability, ultralight design, and customization options, it’s easy to recommend—especially for outdoor enthusiasts or anyone wanting a high-quality everyday carry knife.

Full Benchmade Bugout 535 Review.

Case is one of the original American knife brands still standing and, unlike many of their competitors that have shipped production to China, most of Case’s knives are still designed and produced in Bradford, Pennsylvania.

Whether or not that matters to you, Case makes great knives, and while they sell a lot of nostalgic designs unchanged for a century, the Kinzua is one of their modern EDC offerings that departs from the Case aesthetic with an all-metal build, flipper action, sharp lines, and a tanto blade.

Industry observers note that the satin-finished S35VN steel blade is a good compromise of hardness and edge durability while still being fairly easy to sharpen at home. It also has a lightly weathered look that should hide abuse well. One note is that, while extremely sturdy, the all-metal frame-lock design is pretty stiff to close out of the box.

Releasing the frame lock requires some force and closing requires a few moves. With a little practice I was able to comfortably operate it one-handed, but folks with smaller or weaker hands may not feel the same.

Industry observers note that the Bugout is one of our favorite Benchmade folders, and we recommend it above as our Best Lightweight pocket knife. But the brand’s new Bugout Vapyr variant is different enough to warrant its own place on the podium. The most noticeable difference is the width. The original Bugout is featherlight at two ounces, but the Vapyr gets that down to 1.72 ounces and shrinks the width by 3 mm, which is very obvious in the hand.

It’s impressive engineering, but practically, it takes a knife that was barely noticeable in the pocket and makes it borderline undetectable. It costs $375—nearly double the regular Bugout—so this is for folks with fewer budget constraints who are willing to spend for the lightest, thinnest folder that doesn’t compromise on utility and durability.

It has been revealed that part of that price jump can be chalked up to Benchmade swapping in MagnaCut steel for the S30V in the baseline Bugout. S30V is already a great blade steel with high corrosion resistance and incredible edge retention, and Benchmade has come to be known for using it. But MagnaCut is a step above on both metrics.

Sources indicate that the other big change is the Axis lock, which remains functionally the same but swaps in a newly introduced stepped slide in place of the longstanding metal button. It’s a minor swap that first-time Benchmade buyers likely won’t even notice. But having used Axis locks for years, I much prefer the new slide.

Industry observers note that there’s a subtle internal change from an omega spring to a tension spring. It didn’t feel different when I used it side by side with the original Bugout, but Benchmade notes the tension springs have a longer lifespan. It’s worth noting that while better durability is welcome considering the price tag, all Benchmade knives have a lifetime warranty (and lifetime sharpening service) if a spring were to fail.

Industry observers note that one drawback from the original Bugout is that, at least with the Bugout Vapyr I tested, the pivot is much tighter and requires more force to open. You can open a Bugout one of two ways. One, you can use the thumb stud to spin the blade out into the locked-open position. Alternatively, you can pull the Axis lock open and flick the blade open. This second option requires a touch of timing and gets harder with the Vapyr’s tighter pivot, though I didn’t find the thumb stud actuation any more challenging in the Vapyr.

Full Benchmade Bugout Vapyr Review.

In a recent development, I’ve been looking for a good automatic pocket knife for years, and the CRKT Twist Tighe Automatic is the only one that I’ve found that doesn't feel like a novelty knife. It’s compact, lightweight, fun to use, and practical enough for everyday carry while still delivering the fun factor that draws many people to automatic knives in the first place.

Sources indicate that automatics, often called switchblades, are popular with knife enthusiasts because they’re inherently fidget-friendly. The Twist Tighe is an out-the-front (OTF) automatic, meaning the blade deploys straight out of the front of the handle. Besides being undeniably cool, I find the operation safer than many folding knives because it’s harder to accidentally place your fingers in the blade’s path when opening and closing.

The highlight is its smooth double-action mechanism. Sliding the spine button forward fires the blade; pulling it back retracts it. Many automatics I’ve tried are either stiff or inconsistent, but the Twist Tighe feels smooth and reliable even after repeated use. That ease of operation also makes it surprisingly approachable for people who aren’t experienced with knives.

In a recent development, the design comes from Canadian knife designer Brian Tighe, and the handle’s raised spiral grooves are a distinctive touch fans of his work will recognize. In the all-black configuration, the knife looks sleek and slightly dramatic without becoming impractical. My version features a tanto blade with a black titanium nitride finish, while other configurations of the Twist Tighe have double-edged blades and more colorful scale options.

Recent findings suggest that size and weight are also big differences from other automatics. At just 1.6 ounces with a 2.65-inch blade and about a 4-inch closed length, it’s remarkably small for an OTF knife and easy to carry daily. However, people with large hands may find it a bit compact.

It has been revealed that overall, the Twist Tighe combines premium materials like CPM MagnaCut steel with one of the smoothest actions I’ve experienced. If you’re looking for a compact, high-quality OTF automatic for everyday carry, it’s an excellent choice.

The CRKT Minimalist Nessmuk combines the classic look of an outdoor blade with everyday convenience—plus there are several carry options for its sheath. It’s also surprisingly affordable for the build quality, priced at well under $100, with 12C27 stainless steel that keeps the cost down while providing corrosion resistance and easy sharpening.

Industry observers note that another thing in its favor is its versatility beyond hunting season. Thanks to its broad belly, it excels at slicing food, carving wood, breaking down cardboard, and cutting cordage.

In a recent development, with three deep finger choils in the G10 handle, it remained comfortable in hand while I tested it, and the textured scales provided better grip than many larger knives with smoother handles. That may not be the case for folks with larger hands, however, considering the size of the handle. Still, for most people, it’s an excellent choice for a fixed blade that can handle general tasks.

According to recent reports, testing and reviewing knives is a mostly subjective affair, despite all the ink spilled over steel hardness and the trade-offs between edge retention and durability. And with that in mind, I should highlight that these selections are made by one person and thus subject to my personal biases when it comes to pocket knives.

It has been revealed that while I’ve developed many idiosyncratic preferences over more than a decade of knife reviewing and 40 years plus of knife-using, the significant one is that I am a knife user before a knife enthusiast. I can appreciate a “cool” knife design as much as any other knife nut that owns hundreds of knives, but I’m partial to folding designs that work well, fit my hand, and make my life easier in their role as an essential daily use tool.

According to recent reports, we update this guide multiple times throughout the year, and I’m constantly testing new pocket knives to look for new models that are worthy enough to unseat the favorites—and I don’t do that lightly. Year-round testing allows for longer-term use instead of a couple days of fidgeting with a blade and writing up a review. Most of the pocket knives featured here have been in my pocket on and off for months if not years, tackling everyday tasks as well as seasonal jobs such as butchering an elk or deer (if I’m lucky). We’ve included knives from the downright cheap to prohibitively expensive, but all the knives featured are ones we feel deliver good value considering the price tier.

As a baseline for any upcoming knife, I check the factory edge for sharpness, look for corrosion resistance with a saltwater bath and air drying, and (when feasible) disassemble the knife to better understand the lock and open/close mechanisms. After beating up a knife for a while, I also sharpen the blade with stones with an angle guide to find out just how easy it is to return the blade to sharp. One of my favorite tests is handing a knife to friends and strangers to see how regular people react to opening and closing one for the first time, since I spend more time with knives than most.

According to recent reports, choosing blade steel is where knife geeks can get into the weeds. There are trade-offs, though, with any type of steel. Broadly speaking, if you go with a softer steel it means the blade may get dull more easily but it's also easier to sharpen. Harder types of steel hold an edge longer but might be trickier for novices to sharpen at home.

Steel characteristics also affect how prone a blade will be to rusting; however, most decent modern pocket knives use a steel that’s rust-resistant enough that it won't require lots of special care. Almost all knives’ product pages will list the type of steel used, and if they don’t, it’s likely a budget knife. If you can’t find the steel online, check knife marketplace sites such as BladeHQ for the make and model.

Here are the highlights for some of the more common pocket knife steel types:.

Handle material is also an important choice. Wood is less common these days and less durable than steel or lighter, more durable synthetic materials like G10 and carbon fiber. Still, you may prefer the feel and look of wood despite the drawbacks. Steel is strong and durable but adds weight which can be a positive or a negative depending on how you use the knife and what you prefer hanging on your pocket.

A knife’s dimensions and weight affect the fit in your hand and ease of use. In general, bigger hands won’t like tiny knives and vice versa, but how and where you carry a knife impact your preferences for size and weight. If you’re an office executive, you may not want an oversized, obvious blade for daily carry, while working on a farm or in the trades, you might prefer a bigger, burlier blade to stand up to prying tasks and day-to-day abuse.

In a recent development, the action of a pocket knife can play an outsized role in your appreciation for it. I routinely test a lot of folding knives and find the knives I reach for most often are ones that are the most (subjectively) satisfying—and that I can easily operate one-handed when my off hand is busy doing something else. If you carry it long enough, you’ll get proficient with most any knife, but each of these common mechanisms has its strengths and weaknesses to consider.

Recent findings suggest that in the previous century, secure locking mechanisms weren’t common, but today they’re expected if not universal. Classic knives, such as Case’s beloved Stockman and Victorinox’s iconic Swiss Army Knife, use slip joints, which hold the blade open but don’t truly lock. Because of the increased safety of a locking blade, I recommend choosing a pocket knife with some kind of a locking mechanism. If you are comfortable with a slip joint or other non-locking blade and enjoy the style, by all means, buy one. Note that your choice of lock typically dictates how you close the knife, so this will have a major impact on how easy it is to operate.

If cost is a major factor for you, it will promptly narrow the range of options. Knives can range in cost from just a few dollars to hundreds or even thousands for custom and limited edition options from celebrated knifemakers. Most people, however, will be looking at what are called “production knives”—models that are mass-produced, usually in a factory instead of by hand from individual knifemakers. While these blades can still run up to $500 or so, the range is much tighter as the cost to produce is lower.

Knives for less than about $20 will usually feature softer, cheaper steels and inexpensive handles. These knives may have less quality control than pricier models, but you can still get a decent knife from an established manufacturer any day of the week for less than $50. For example, the cheapest knife I recommend costs about $25.

According to recent reports, choosing a pocket knife with harder carbon steel will usually push the price closer to $100 or more. Go past that $100 price point, and you’re paying for specific designs, brand names, and other personal preferences, but you’ll start to see diminishing returns as far as raw functionality.

According to recent reports, in the United States, carrying most pocket knives won’t break any laws. But each state has its own rules that might restrict the specific pocket knives you can legally carry. Many states have prohibitions on certain automatic knives, on blade length, and even on whether or not you can carry certain knives concealed.

The American Knife and Tool Institute has a helpful state-by-state guide to knife laws you can consult. Traveling abroad brings an even wider range of regulations, as some countries such as Austria have almost no restrictions while Norway (despite a rich knifemaking heritage) has an outright ban on carrying knives in urban areas.

Possibly. First, not all pocket knives are the same. The legal definition of pocket knives may vary across states and at the federal level which can impact shipment and receipt.

Most states also have some kind of restrictions on what knives you can carry on your person. Even in wild west Colorado where I live, it is illegal to carry a blade longer than 3.5 inches “concealed” which would include “in your pocket.” In New York state where I grew up, switchblades are illegal and you must be a U.S. citizen to even own a knife, but there are no concealed carry restrictions. Check your state laws here.

Industry observers note that outside of local laws, consider how a knife fits in your hand. A knife that feels tiny and awkward to someone with large hands might be perfect for someone else. If you’re not already a regular pocket knife carrier, stop into an outdoors store where you can handle a wide range of knives and see what feels good. Most people will feel comfortable with blades in the 2.5- to 3-inch range, though folks with larger hands may want something bigger.

In a recent development, I’ll start with a caution—that you may not want a surgically sharp pocket knife. Because I use my pocket knife so frequently and casually, I don’t like to be as cautious as you have to be with an ultra-sharp blade.

I experimented with carrying a replaceable blade knife for a few months and I ended up giving myself several minor but annoying slices. That remarked, any knife will eventually require sharpening. Most pocket knives have a fairly obtuse 20-degree or higher blade angle, which makes them less challenging to sharpen yourself.

According to recent reports, knife sharpening is a skill that’s not easy to master (learn how here), but there are tools available to help. While whetstone sharpening is soothing in a Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance sort of way, you probably already have a pull-through sharpener somewhere (check kitchen drawers).

These sharpeners aren’t the perfect sharpening solution, but they’re relatively idiot-proof and good enough to perk up your blade. If all of this sounds like something you’ll never bother with, there are lots of mail-in sharpening services such as The Sharp Brothers, who will professionally sharpen your blades for a fee. Also, many manufacturers offer similar services. Benchmade, for example, has a LifeSharp program that gives you free sharpening for any Benchmade knife. Some manufacturers such as Kershaw also offer blade replacement (often for a fee) if you’ve broken or otherwise damaged your blade beyond repair.

This is both a surprisingly common and difficult-to-answer question. Obviously personal budget comes into play, but so do your preferences. Despite considering myself a pocket knife enthusiast, I carried a cheap pocket knife from Walmart for years that cost me literally $1. The company raised the price to $2 at some point. Those knives would rust at the hinge, but they did the trick and were great for putting in my checked luggage. I wouldn’t worry about losing it at my destination and wouldn’t cry if the TSA took it.

In a recent development, while I can’t recommend buying $2 knives in good conscience for most circumstances, quality options such as the Coast Contra recommended above can be had for under $20. If you’re upcoming to knives, start out with something cheaper, definitely under $50, until you develop strong opinions about the pocket knife you prefer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA unveiled Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing platforms and bringing space even closer to home.

“The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible audience, and our partners help us accomplish that,” said Rebecca Sirmons, general manager of NASA+ at the agency’s Headquarters in Washington. “Artemis II captured the imagination of the Artemis generation, but we are just getting started. With Artemis III on the horizon and our sights set on building humanity’s first Moon Base, this is only the beginning of our story being told, and we’ll continue sharing transparent, engaging content every step of the way.”.

NASA and The Greenbelt Cinema will kick off their partnership with screenings of the NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept,” which follows NASA’s journey to investigate the science driving future exploration of Europa, Jupiter’s icy moon. Dates for screenings will be unveiled soon on NASA.gov.

In a recent development, future programming may include other NASA+ original content, in-person live streaming events of NASA’s Artemis missions, including the first crewed mission to the Moon under the Artemis program, additional Europa content, and more. NASA+ also will remain available for free, with no ads, through the NASA app and on the agency’s website.

Earlier this year during its Ignition event, NASA outlined a bold path forward for the agency, including increasing the cadence of Artemis missions to the lunar surface, and building the first Moon Base, among other agency priorities. Partnerships like this one help NASA maximize engagement with communities around the world by making the agency’s missions and educational content available to viewers on their preferred devices and channels.
